The SanDisk 512 GB MicroSD Express card works with Nintendo Switch 2 and uses the PCIe and NVMe interfaces to reach speeds of up to 650 MB/s and write speeds of up to 220 MB/s.

The MicroSD Express standard is fairly latest. Because of this, the heightened prices of NAND mean that typical prices for cards such as these have remained high. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding.
  • Check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL!
  • According to recent reports, llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Llama Nemotron Nano VL is a state-of-the-art 8B Vision Language Model (VLM) designed for intelligent document processing, offering high accuracy and multimodal understanding. Available on Hugging Face, it excels in extracting and understanding information from complex documents like invoices, receipts, contracts, and more. With its powerful OCR capabilities and efficient performance on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, this model delivers industry-leading accuracy for text and table extraction, as well as chart, diagram, and table parsing. Whether you’re automating financial document processing or improving business intelligence workflows, Llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for fast, scalable deployments.

Check out the tutorial below to start building your own intelligent document processing solutions with Llama Nemotron Nano VL! Users can also post-train the model further with their own datasets using NVIDIA NeMo.

According to recent reports, llama Nemotron Nano VL, the latest addition to the NVIDIA Nemotron family of models, is a vision language model (VLM) designed to push the boundaries of intelligent document processing (IDP) and optical character recognition (OCR). With its high accuracy, low model footprint, and multimodal capabilities, Llama Nemotron Nano VL enables the seamless extraction and understanding of information from complex documents. This includes PDFs, images, tables, charts, formulas, and diagrams, making it an ideal solution for automating document workflows across various industries like finance, healthcare, legal, and government.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL demonstrates exceptional accuracy on the OCRBench v2 benchmark, which tests models on real-world OCR and document understanding tasks. These tasks include text recognition, table extraction, and element parsing across various document types. The model’s advanced capabilities enable it to deliver better performance than current leading VLMs in real-world enterprise scenarios.

Industry observers note that llama Nemotron Nano VL builds upon Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and C-RADIOv2-VLM-H, a Vision Transformer (ViT) that serves as the backbone for visual feature extraction. This allows the model to handle a wide variety of visual elements in documents, including charts, graphs, and other complex visual representations.

It has been revealed that C-RADIOv2-VLM-H Vision Transformer (ViT): The core visual understanding component of the model, C-RADIO allows for high-resolution processing of documents containing complex visual elements. This serves as a vision backbone, excelling across visual domains and enabling the model to process multi-image understanding with high resolution. This technology underpins the model’s ability to handle complex documents containing visual elements such as images, diagrams, charts, and tables.

It has been revealed that C-RADIO is trained on multi-resolution data using multiple distillation techniques. Multiplicative noise was applied to our weights during training to improve generalization.

Sources indicate that llama Nemotron VL further adopts a design that dynamically aggregates encoded patch features, enabling support for high-resolution input without sacrificing spatial continuity. This strategy efficiently processes documents with arbitrary aspect ratios while preserving both local detail and global context. It enables fine-grained analysis of dense visual content—such as small fonts, multi-column layouts, and intricate charts—without compromising computational efficiency or coverage. The model can also preserve the information better and have less distortion, due to the innovation in high-resolution tiling.

By empowering Llama-3.1 8B LLM with this strong vision foundation, Llama Nemotron Nano VL delivers unparalleled accuracy in parsing and interpreting documents.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using several OSS datasets along with data from NVIDIA’s VLM-based OCR solution, NeMo Retriever Parse. This provides capabilities in text and table parsing, along with grounding, enabling the Llama Nemotron Nano VL to perform at an industry-leading level in document understanding tasks. Synthetic table extraction datasets that were used for training this OCR solution were also used for training Llama Nemotron Nano VL 8B VLM to enable more optimal table understanding and extraction.

Recent findings suggest that llama Nemotron Nano VL excels in tasks like text recognition and visual reasoning, and demonstrates advanced chart and diagram understanding capabilities. Llama Nemotron Nano VL allows for predicting bounding box coordinates in normalized space to enable grounding like tasks and text-referring.

Recent findings suggest that this strong performance is underpinned by high-quality in-domain data combined with a diverse training distribution across document types, languages, and layouts. A robust data strategy ensures coverage across challenging use cases through selective curation, targeted augmentation, and formatting techniques that clarify task intent and reduce ambiguity—resulting in models that generalize effectively to real-world applications.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL undergoes a two-stage training regimen: pre-training followed by Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The initial pre-training phase focuses on achieving cross-modal alignment between the language and vision domains. This is accomplished through the training of a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) connector, which serves as an interface between the two modalities.

For the training process, Llama Nemotron Nano VL leverages a comprehensive and diverse collection of datasets. This aggregated dataset, comprising a total of ~1.5M samples, includes publicly available, synthetically generated, as well as internally curated datasets. A summary of the datasets utilized during the pre-training stage is presented in Figure 1.

In a recent development, in the Supervised Fine-Tuning stage, Llama-Nemotron-Nano-VL is trained end-to-end on a combination of synthetic, public, and internally curated datasets. The data encompasses a wide spectrum of tasks, including but not limited to: OCR, text grounding, table parsing, and general document-based VQA.

The document understanding capabilities of Llama Nemotron Nano VL can be largely attributed to the OCR-focused SFT data blend. Besides simple OCR, many of the datasets involve tasks such as predicting the correct reading order, reconstructing markdown formatting along with semantic classes (such as Captions, Titles, Section headers) and bounding boxes of individual text blocks. The model is also trained to parse mathematical formulas in LaTeX format and to extract tables in LaTeX, HTML, or markdown formats, depending on the prompt.

To ensure robustness across various domains, we apply affine and photometric augmentations to the document images. To improve the table and chart parsing performance further, we enable swapping of tables and charts embedded into the full-page documents between the datasets. This enables the model to handle diverse document layouts and structures.

In a recent development, A large portion of the internally-created datasets are based on Nemo Retriever Parse training data. These include NVPDFTex - a collection of arxiv documents with ground-truth labels consisting of formatted text in reading order, with bounding boxes and semantic classes of text, as well as LaTeX tables and equations; Common Crawl pdfs that are labeled by human annotators; rendered text from Wikipedia with markdown formatting and tables, as well as a number of synthetic datasets targeted at improving table parsing capabilities and dense OCR. In addition, the training blend includes a number of publicly-available datasets, such as DocLayNet, FinTabNet and PubTables-1M, in which we refine the groundtruth labels.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2 below reveals the task distribution of the training data. As can be seen, a significant portion of the training samples involve OCR along with grounding and table parsing, as well as OCR-adjacent VQA tasks.

Industry observers note that llama Nemotron Nano VL was trained using NVIDIA Megatron and utilizes efficient Transformer implementations in NVIDIA Transformer Engine. For multimodal dataloading, we use Megatron Energon. We provide example Megatron training and inference scripts along with hyperparameters and other instructions to enable custom training of VLMs.

Sources indicate that to ensure the output is formatted precisely as you need, we recommend including detailed instructions within your prompts. We've provided some examples below to illustrate how this works for various tasks:.

In a recent development, OCRBench v2 is an advanced benchmark designed to evaluate OCR models across a diverse range of real-world document types and layouts. It includes over 10,000 human-verified question-answer pairs to rigorously assess a model’s capabilities in visual text localization, table parsing, diagram reasoning and key-value extraction.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL outperforms other VLMs on this benchmark and also achieves strong accuracies in benchmarks such as ChartQA and AI2D, making it a compelling option for enterprises aiming to automate document workflows such as:.

Its combination of high accuracy, strong layout aware reasoning, and efficient deployment on a single GPU makes it an ideal choice for large-scale enterprise automation.

In a recent development, llama Nemotron Nano VL is optimized for various document processing tasks across multiple industries. Here are some of the key use cases where the model excels:.

Sources indicate that automating the extraction of line items, totals, dates, and other key data points from invoices and receipts. This is crucial for accounting, ERP integration, and expense management.

Extracting structured data from passports, IDs, and tax forms for regulatory compliance and KYC processes.

Automatically identifying key clauses, dates, and obligations in legal documents.

Extracting patient data, claim information, and policy details from medical records and insurance forms.

Llama Nemotron Nano VL provides developers with the tools to automate document processing workflows at scale. It is available through the NVIDIA NIM API and for download on Hugging Face, where you can begin building production-ready document understanding applications. Users can also use NVIDIA NeMo to finetune the model on their own dataset.

Hardware hacker BigCrimping (Crimp) has made a dedicated portable Wi-Fi NAS that allows for easily reading and copying 3.5" floppy disks over a network. The renaissance of vintage hardware also extends to some early digital cameras, like the Sony Mavica and Panasonic PV-SD families. These point-and-shooters were popular due to using bog-standard 3.5" floppies in PC format. Many folks may still have floppies from this era around, or simply want to breathe fresh life into their cameras.

Recent findings suggest that the fresh device is called floppy3.5, and its design is completely open-source. Making one ought to be pretty easy, as Crimp made all the required files available on GitHub, including data for 3D printing the enclosure, and a custom PCB with an RP2354A microcontroller and an ESP32-S3 bridge. Besides those items, you'll need predictable necessities like a battery, a slimline floppy drive, a Wi-Fi module, and a microSD slot.

Sources indicate that the onboard monochrome LCD display looks pretty handy, as Crimp made it show a bevy of information, including sector and cylinder counts, a good/bad sector map, file counts, and even a firmware upgrade progress counter. The onboard buttons do what they say: READ to scan the files, or SAVE to dump them to an SD card. The DISP and POWER buttons return you to the home screen, and power the device off and on.

Industry observers note that the card in remarked slot optionally stores the disk's files, allowing you to easily go around a storeroom or attic and just insert floppies one after another for archival without needing a computer. When it's time to manage content, you can access the floppy3.5's web interface over the network, and even connect to it directly with a USB cable if you need fancier features like fetching entire disk images.

In a recent development, crimp chose to use the Greaseweazle floppy drive comms protocol instead of relying on a conventional floppy drive controller. Besides saving on hardware, this allows full control over the drive, as Greaseweazle manages a drive's wire signals directly, making for easy imaging and all sorts of direct data manipulation, regardless of a disk's underlying format. By default, floppy3.5 understands FAT12 for its main purpose, but you can use the Greaseweazle utilities over the cable if needed.

Sources indicate that sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training dense embedding, reranker (cross encoder), and sparse embedding models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, paraphrase mining, and more. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a sparse encoder/embedding model and explain why you might want to do so. This results in sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq, a cheap model that works especially well in hybrid search or retrieve and rerank scenarios.

Finetuning sparse embedding models involves several components: the model, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong sparse embedding models.

According to recent reports, in addition to training your own models, you can choose from a wide range of pretrained sparse encoders available on the Hugging Face Hub. To help navigate this growing space, we’ve curated a SPLADE Models collection highlighting some of the most relevant models.We list the most prominent ones along with their benchmark results in Pretrained Models in the documentation.

The broader term "embedding models" refer to models that convert some input, usually text, into a vector representation (embedding) that captures the semantic meaning of the input. Unlike with the raw inputs, you can perform mathematical operations on these embeddings, resulting in similarity scores that can be used for various tasks, such as search, clustering, or classification.

It has been revealed that with dense embedding models, i.e. the common variety, the embeddings are typically low-dimensional vectors (e.g., 384, 768, or 1024 dimensions) where most values are non-zero. Sparse embedding models, on the other hand, produce high-dimensional vectors (e.g., 30,000+ dimensions) where most values are zero. Usually, each active dimension (i.e. the dimension with a non-zero value) in a sparse embedding corresponds to a specific token in the model's vocabulary, allowing for interpretability.

Let's have a look at naver/splade-v3, a state-of-the-art sparse embedding model, as an example:.

In this example, the embeddings are 30,522-dimensional vectors, where each dimension corresponds to a token in the model's vocabulary. The decode method returned the top 10 tokens with the highest values in the embedding, allowing us to interpret which tokens contribute most to the embedding.

We can even determine the intersection or overlap between embeddings, very useful for determining why two texts are deemed similar or dissimilar:.

A key component of neural sparse embedding models is query/document expansion. Unlike traditional lexical methods like BM25, which only match exact tokens, neural sparse models generally automatically expand the original text with semantically related terms:.

For example, in the code output above, the sentence "The weather is lovely today" is expanded to include terms like "beautiful", "cool", "pretty", and "nice" which weren't in the original text. Similarly, "It's so sunny outside!" is expanded to include "weather", "summer", and "sun".

Recent findings suggest that this expansion allows neural sparse models to match semantically related content or synonyms even without exact token matches, handle misspellings, and overcome vocabulary mismatch problems. This is why neural sparse models like SPLADE often outperform traditional lexical search methods while maintaining the efficiency benefits of sparse representations.

However, expansion has its risks. For example, query expansion for "What is the weather on Tuesday?" will likely also expand to "monday", "wednesday", etc., which may not be desired.

Recent findings suggest that in short, neural sparse embedding models fall in a valuable niche between traditional lexical methods like BM25 and dense embedding models like Sentence Transformers. They have the following advantages:.

Throughout this blogpost, I'll use "sparse embedding model" and "sparse encoder model" interchangeably.

Industry observers note that the majority of (neural) sparse embedding models employ the aforementioned query/document expansion so that you can match texts with nearly identical meaning, even if they don't share any words. In short, the model has to recognize synonyms so those tokens can be placed in the final embedding.

Most out-of-the-box sparse embedding models will easily recognize that "supermarket", "food", and "market" are useful expansions of a text containing "grocery", but for example:.

Sources indicate that whereas we wish for it to expand to "headache", the common word for "cephalalgia". This example expands to many domains, e.g. not recognizing that "Java" is a programming language, that "Audi" makes cars, or that "NVIDIA" is a manufacturer that makes graphics cards.

Through finetuning, the model can learn to focus exclusively on the domain and/or language that matters to you.

Training Sentence Transformer models involves the following components:.

Now, let's dive into each of these components in more detail.

Sparse Encoder models consist of a sequence of Modules, Sparse Encoder specific Modules or Custom Modules, allowing for a lot of flexibility. If you want to further finetune a Sparse Encoder model (e.g. it has a modules.json file), then you don't have to worry about which modules are used:.

But if instead you want to train from another checkpoint, or from scratch, then these are the most common architectures you can use:.

Recent findings suggest that splade models use the MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling modules. The former loads a pretrained Masked Language Modeling transformer model (e.g. BERT, RoBERTa, DistilBERT, ModernBERT, etc.) and the latter pools the output of the MLMHead to produce a single sparse embedding of the size of the vocabulary.

This architecture is the default if you provide a fill-mask model architecture to SparseEncoder, so it's easier to use the shortcut:.

According to recent reports, inference-free Splade uses a Router module with different modules for queries and documents. Usually for this type of architecture, the documents part is a traditional Splade architecture (a MLMTransformer followed by a SpladePooling module) and the query part is an SparseStaticEmbedding module, which just returns a pre-computed score for every token in the query.

This architecture allows for fast query-time processing using the lightweight SparseStaticEmbedding approach, that can be trained and seen as a linear weights, while documents are processed with the full MLM transformer and SpladePooling.

Inference-free Splade is particularly useful for search applications where query latency is critical, as it shifts the computational complexity to the document indexing phase which can be done offline.

Sources indicate that when training models with the Router module, you must use the router_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map the training dataset columns to the correct route ("query" or "document"). For example, if your dataset(s) have ["question", "answer"] columns, then you can use the following mapping:.

According to recent reports, additionally, it is recommended to use a much higher learning rate for the SparseStaticEmbedding module than for the rest of the model. For this, you should use the learning_rate_mapping argument in the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments to map parameter patterns to their learning rates. For example, if you want to use a learning rate of 1e-3 for the SparseStaticEmbedding module and 2e-5 for the rest of the model, you can do this:.

Contrastive Sparse Representation (CSR) models, introduced in Beyond Matryoshka: Revisiting Sparse Coding for Adaptive Representation, apply a SparseAutoEncoder module on top of a dense Sentence Transformer model, which usually consist of a Transformer followed by a Pooling module. You can initialize one from scratch like so:.

Or if your base model is 1) a dense Sentence Transformer model or 2) a non-MLM Transformer model (those are loaded as Splade models by default), then this shortcut will automatically initialize the CSR model for you:.

Unlike (Inference-free) Splade models, sparse embeddings by CSR models don't have the same size as the vocabulary of the base model. This means you can't directly interpret which words are activated in your embedding like you can with Splade models, where each dimension corresponds to a specific token in the vocabulary.

Sources indicate that beyond that, CSR models are most effective on dense encoder models that use high-dimensional representations (e.g. 1024-4096 dimensions).

It has been revealed that the SparseEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in various formats such as CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL.

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets in the Hugging Face Hub.

In a recent development, some datasets, like nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual, have multiple subsets with different data formats. You need to specify the subset name along with the dataset name, e.g. dataset = load_dataset("nthakur/swim-ir-monolingual", "de", split="train").

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in certain file formats:.

You can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict if your local data requires pre-processing. This allows you to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:.

Each key in the dictionary becomes a column in the resulting dataset.

Sources indicate that it's crucial to ensure that your dataset format matches your chosen loss function. This involves checking two things:.

For example, if your loss function accepts (anchor, positive, negative) triplets, then your first, second, and third dataset columns correspond with anchor, positive, and negative, respectively. This means that your first and second column must contain texts that should embed closely, and that your first and third column must contain texts that should embed far apart. That is why depending on your loss function, your dataset column order matters.

Consider a dataset with columns ["text1", "text2", "label"], where the "label" column contains floating point similarity scores. This dataset can be used with SparseCoSENTLoss, SparseAnglELoss, and SparseCosineSimilarityLoss because:.

If the columns in your dataset are not ordered correctly, use Dataset.select_columns to reorder them. Additionally, remove any extraneous columns (e.g., sample_id, metadata, source, type) using Dataset.remove_columns, as they will be treated as inputs otherwise.

Loss functions measure how well a model performs on a given batch of data and guide the optimization process. The choice of loss function depends on your available data and target task. Refer to the Loss Overview for a comprehensive list of options.

According to recent reports, to train a SparseEncoder, you either need a SpladeLoss or CSRLoss, depending on the architecture. These are wrapper losses that add sparsity regularization on top of a main loss function, which must be provided as a parameter. The only loss that can be used independently is SparseMSELoss, as it performs embedding-level distillation, ensuring sparsity by directly copying the teacher's sparse embedding.

Most loss functions can be initialized with just the SparseEncoder that you're training, alongside some optional parameters, e.g.:.

It has been revealed that the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments class allows you to specify parameters that influence training performance and tracking/debugging. While optional, experimenting with these arguments can help improve training efficiency and provide insights into the training process.

In a recent development, in the Sentence Transformers documentation, I've outlined some of the most useful training arguments. I would recommend reading it in Training Overview > Training Arguments.

Here's an example of how to initialize SparseEncoderTrainingArguments:.

It has been revealed that note that eval_strategy was introduced in transformers version 4.41.0. Prior versions should use evaluation_strategy instead.

It has been revealed that you can provide the SparseEncoderTrainer with an eval_dataset to get the evaluation loss during training, but it may be useful to get more concrete metrics during training, too. For this, you can use evaluators to assess the model's performance with useful metrics before, during, or after training. You can use both an eval_dataset and an evaluator, one or the other, or neither. They evaluate based on the eval_strategy and eval_steps Training Arguments.

Here are the implemented Evaluators that come with Sentence Transformers for Sparse Encoder models:.

Additionally, SequentialEvaluator should be used to combine multiple evaluators into one Evaluator that can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainer.

According to recent reports, sometimes you don't have the required evaluation data to prepare one of these evaluators on your own, but you still want to track how well the model performs on some common benchmarks. In that case, you can use these evaluators with data from Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that when evaluating frequently during training with a small eval_steps, consider using a tiny eval_dataset to minimize evaluation overhead. If you're concerned about the evaluation set size, a 90-1-9 train-eval-test split can provide a balance, reserving a reasonably sized test set for final evaluations. After training, you can assess your model's performance using trainer.evaluate(test_dataset) for test loss or initialize a testing evaluator with test_evaluator(model) for detailed test metrics.

If you evaluate after training, but before saving the model, your automatically generated model card will still include the test results.

When using Distributed Training, the evaluator only runs on the first device, unlike the training and evaluation datasets, which are shared across all devices.

The SparseEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. We only have to specify the trainer with the model, training arguments (optional), training dataset, evaluation dataset (optional), loss function, evaluator (optional) and we can start training. Let’s have a look at a script where all of these components come together:.

Industry observers note that after running this script, the sparse-encoder/example-inference-free-splade-distilbert-base-uncased-nq model was uploaded for me. The model scores 0.5241 NDCG@10 on NanoMSMARCO, 0.3299 NDCG@10 on NanoNFCorpus and 0.5357 NDCG@10 NanoNQ, which is a good result for an inference-free distilbert-based model trained on just 100k pairs from the Natural Questions dataset.

The model uses an average of 184 active dimensions in the sparse embeddings for the documents, compared to 7.7 active dimensions for the queries (i.e. the average number of tokens in the query). This corresponds to a sparsity of 99.39% and 99.97%, respectively.

All of this information is stored in the automatically generated model card, including the base model, language, license, evaluation results, training & evaluation dataset info, hyperparameters, training logs, and more. Without any effort, your uploaded models should contain all the information that your potential users would need to determine whether your model is suitable for them.

The Sentence Transformers trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:.

These are automatically used without you having to specify anything, as long as the required dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Top-performing models are often trained using multiple datasets simultaneously. The SparseEncoderTrainer simplifies this process by allowing you to train with multiple datasets without converting them to the same format. You can even apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps for multi-dataset training:.

Sources indicate that each training/evaluation batch will contain samples from only one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is determined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the SparseEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. The valid options are:.

According to recent reports, let's evaluate our newly trained inference-free SPLADE model using the NanoMSMARCO dataset, and see how it compares to dense retrieval approaches. We'll also explore hybrid retrieval methods that combine sparse and dense vectors, as well as reranking to further improve search quality.

It has been revealed that the Sparse and Dense rankings can be combined using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), which is a simple way to combine the results of multiple rankings. If a Reranker is applied, it will rerank the results of the prior retrieval step.

Sources indicate that the results indicate that for this dataset, combining Dense and Sparse rankings is very performant, resulting in 12.3% and 18.7% increases over the Dense and Sparse baselines, respectively. In short, combining Sparse and Dense retrieval methods is a very effective way to improve search performance.

Furthermore, applying a reranker on any of the rankings improved the performance to approximately 66.3 NDCG@10, showing that either Sparse, Dense, or Hybrid (Dense + Sparse) found the relevant documents in their top 100, which the reranker then ranked to the top 10. So, replacing a Dense -> Reranker pipeline with a Sparse -> Reranker pipeline might improve both latency and costs:.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, we shrank 1 GB of Wikipedia to 105.39 MB, losslessly.
  • According to recent reports, researcher Tommy He built tufazip, and the full package, at 105.39MB after optimization, includes a small, 4.33MB pre-trained starter model — stored at low precision, or quantized, to save space — that’s needed to unpack the file.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, tufa Labs’ tufazip has compressed 1GB of information from Wikipedia into just 105MB of space, losslessly, without using any hand-built models, according to a research post. The method uses a 163-million-parameter Transformer model as a predictor instead, and similar compression or decompression would take two Nvidia B200 GPUs about a week to manage. It’s the smallest result on the Large Text Compression Benchmark from any entry that uses a neural network as its only predictor.

In a recent development, we shrank 1 GB of Wikipedia to 105.39 MB, losslessly. Introducing tufazip: the best entry on the Large Text Compression Benchmark using a neural network as its sole predictor. Everything above it mixes a transformer with hand-built models.November 19, 2026.

According to recent reports, researcher Tommy He built tufazip, and the full package, at 105.39MB after optimization, includes a small, 4.33MB pre-trained starter model — stored at low precision, or quantized, to save space — that’s needed to unpack the file. The full model is a 12-layer Transformer, which means there are 12 stages for each guess to go through. The starter stores just two already-trained stages, copying them back and forth to fill all 12 once the full model spins up in memory; each copy keeps learning on its own.

Recent findings suggest that this doesn’t work like a traditional chatbot or cloud AI but is, rather, a self-contained language model that learns on the fly. Notable here is that this compression is lossless, which means there’s no risk of any data being lost in the process. This means that predictor updates must be “fully deterministic.”.

Training happens in two stages. The starter, a 34-million-parameter model, is trained offline, before any compression begins. Then, the full model begins to learn online, by predicting each token and training on it, with the unpacking side repeating the same steps, with the model itself being rebuilt alongside the text. For this reason, the total size must include, besides the compressed text, only the unpacking program and the files it needs, including the starter, but not the full trained model.

According to recent reports, there is no traditional, hand-built compression model that assists, setting it apart, Tufa Labs states, from all 12 entries that now rank above it on the benchmark, which mix a Transformer with hand-built models. Its first, online-only version ranked second when submitted in early September; the 105.39MB version was 13th as of the benchmark’s Nov. 19 update. Emphasis should be placed on this being a text-only benchmark, for those imagining media files.

While this sounds more exciting than, say, WinRAR, it’s for research purposes and not a product, and that’s underlined by what you’d need to actually run it. Currently, two Nvidia B200 GPUs — plus two Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPUs in the test machine — would need 631,548 seconds to compress and 645,748 seconds to decompress the 105.39MB version, or about 7.3 and 7.5 days, respectively, not counting the starter’s offline training.

Industry observers note that the first version, which learned entirely online and came in at 105.98MB, took 647,595 and 630,136 seconds. Its GPUs peaked at 43.37 GiB of VRAM between them, and total memory use, GPUs included, peaked at roughly 68,525 MiB during compression and 73,748 MiB during decompression.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

7.3 days (excl. offline training).

The experiment is fundamentally interesting because it reveals, for example, that a smaller vocabulary can actually help: a 4K-word tokenizer beats both 8K and 16K. Giving Wikipedia’s XML markup its own dedicated tokens made the compression worse. Bigger isn’t always better, and that goes for model size, too, as a 267-million-parameter model did slightly worse than a 188-million-parameter model on this data set. With a smaller, 100MB version of the file, gains leveled off at about 77 million parameters. A run started from a bigger, six-layer offline model predicted better, with just a 99.17MB payload, but its chunkier weights made the total file larger than the online-only run.

Sources indicate that improving compression can be costly, as widening the window of already-processed text used for extra training, from 15 to 35 million tokens, only cut the payload 1.21% at the cost of 40% more compute. The key takeaways are that optimization isn’t always as simple as throwing more at the problem, and that trade-offs can be more expensive than expected. He frames that six-layer trade-off as the next research question: how much predictive quality a smaller model can keep, which makes the vanishing point a balance between predictive quality and model size for this benchmark.

Most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.
  • Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!
  • The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

🔗Competition website | ✍️Registration form | 💬Discord channel | 📝Competition proposal.

Join us in building benchmarks that capture early-stage reasoning & scientific knowledge in LLMs!

The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) typically begins with a series of ablation experiments, wherein various model architectures, data mixtures, and training hyperparameters are systematically evaluated. This phase is commonly referred to as the early stages of training. During this period, researchers primarily monitor two key metrics: the training loss curve and evaluation scores. However, existing evaluation benchmarks often fail to provide meaningful or discriminative signals during these initial stages where LLMs are trained on a few tokens ~200B tokens, making it challenging to derive conclusive insights from ongoing experiments.

In this competition, we want to build together new benchmarks to effectively capture relevant signals in early training stages of LLMs, specifically for scientific knowledge domain.

According to recent reports, the competition will be hosted on a dedicated Hugging Face organization - to register to the competition please follow this registration link 👉 https://e2lmc.github.io/registration. Participants will have to submit their solutions, which will be based on lm-evaluation-harness library through a HuggingFace Space. An active leaderboard will be maintained during the competition to track promising submissions. The size of the models make them easily runnable for everyone, on free-tier Google Colab GPUs. We also provide a comprehensive starting kit including several notebooks to get started with the competition.

In a recent development, each submission will be evaluated using three different scores: signal quality score (ScoreSQ), ranking consistency score (ScoreRC) amd compliance with scientific knowledge score (ScoreCS). These criteria will be combined into a global score used for the final ranking. Additionally, two validation procedures will be systematically applied to all submissions: (i) verification of alignment with established scientific knowledge domains, and (ii) detection of potential information leakage, specifically the presence of the answer within the question prompt.The overall score is computed as a weighted sum:.

where, αSQ, αRC and αCS are weighting coefficients that reflect the relative importance of each criterion. We set the weights as α1 = 0.5, α2 = 0.1 and α3 = 0.4, thereby placing greater emphasis on signal quality and compliance to scientific knowledge, which we consider the most vital metrics in evaluating submissions.

Participants will be able to compute the signal quality subscore locally using the provided model checkpoints of three Small Language Models 0.5B, 1B and 3B (ranging from 0 to 200 BT) along with the accompanying scoring algorithm (provided in a notebook in the starting kit). In contrast, the other two subscores cannot be computed independently, as the corresponding checkpoints—from 200 GT to 1 T tokens, as well as the 0.5 billion parameter model trained exclusively on web data—will remain hidden throughout the competition. Nonetheless, the global score will be automatically computed upon submission through the Hugging Face competition space, allowing participants to track their overall performance. This setup is intended to prevent overly customized solutions specifically tailored to the released checkpoints.

Further details about each evaluation metric, along with full scoring results on state-of-the-art benchmarks, are available in the competition proposal.

For inquiries and support, reach out to the task coordinators at e2lmc@tii.ae. You can also join our discord channel here to directly interact with us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI has taken over everything in the past few years, with AI features bombarding virtually every app or service available. If you’ve ever wanted to just turn off AI features, Canva proves that it could be a simple toggle, if companies actually wanted to give you a choice.

Canva today revealed “AI Controls,” a latest toggle that completely turns off generative AI features within the editing app.

Sources indicate that generative AI can be quite helpful in working on posters, editing images, and more, but it’s not everyone’s preference. Canva puts this well:.

According to recent reports, for some people, AI is the most exciting creative tool in a generation, while others prefer bringing their ideas to life without it. We believe the future of creativity should give everyone the freedom to choose their own path, whether that’s creating with AI, without it, or somewhere in between.

In a recent development, to give its users the choice, Canva’s Permissions menu now has a simple toggle for “Enable Generative AI features.” Toggling it off disables features such as Magic Write and Magic Edit. There’s also an option to limit how much AI-generated imagery appears in the Canva library.

Put simply, this is great to see.

Sources indicate that AI has its place, but everyone should have a choice like this, especially when it comes to apps and services used for artistry in the same vein as Canva. Yet, the tech industry continues to go in the opposite direction, shoving AI into every corner whether it’s actually useful or not. Canva proves, though, that it doesn’t have to be that way.

Breaking: Efficient MultiModal Data Pipeline

📅 08 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, sound familiar?
  • In this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've got everything ready - data, model, a beefy GPU setup. You hit "run" and... wait. And wait some more. Your GPUs are barely breaking a sweat while your wallet's getting lighter by the hour.

According to recent reports, sound familiar? We've been there. After some detective work on our nanoVLM project, we discovered the real culprit wasn't our model or hardware, it was our data pipeline being incredibly wasteful.

In this post we build an efficient pipeline in five stages. In each stage we add or remove from the previous step and comment on what went right and what did not.

According to recent reports, to make it easier to follow the data preparation tasks, we created a separate repo laser-focused on the data pipeline only. We hope this will be much easier to understand that reading the code once integrated with the nanoVLM repository. In addition, this could be useful to bootstrap other data pipelines!

Repository: https://github.com/ariG23498/mmdp.

According to recent reports, to follow along, all you need to do is clone the repository. It contains the final data preparation tasks, but it's designed to showcase each step of the way.

Before optimizing anything, we need to understand what we are working with. Our multimodal dataset has images, text prompts, and responses.

Getting familiar with your training data is crucial for success. The previous script indicates a random sample each time you run it; you may want to copy the snippet to a notebook and run it multiple times to get a feeling about the data.

Our first training attempt used the obvious (and very frequent) approach:.

In a recent development, the results were painful. Look at this visualization:.

See all that gray? That's padding. That's the GPU processing absolutely nothing while you pay for compute time. We were wasting roughly 60% of our batch on empty tokens.

Recent findings suggest that our next move was simple. Set a global maximum length and stick to it. If a sample was too long, we'd just drop it.

According to recent reports, as you might have noticed that the batch now has one sample less. This is due to the filtering process. This helped, but we were still padding everything to the same fixed length regardless of actual content. Better than before, but still wasteful.

Now we’re ready to rethink batching entirely. Padding is the enemy, and we need a strategy to minimize it while maximizing how much data we can fit into each batch. Enter the knapsack problem, a classic from computer science that’s perfect for this.

In a recent development, imagine you’re packing a backpack for a hike. It can only hold so much weight, and you want to cram in as many useful items as possible. In our case:.

To test this idea, we start with a toy dataset: just a list of numbers from 1 to 25, each representing a sequence length. This lets us experiment without the complexity of images and text.

It has been revealed that most PyTorch datasets are map-style (you access them with dataset[i]). But for dynamic batching, we need something more flexible. So, we built an iterable-style dataset by subclassing torch.utils.data.IterableDataset. This lets us generate batches on the fly and handle tricks like sharding data across multiple workers:.

In a recent development, packing sequences can be slow, especially if we’re sorting or shuffling. To keep things moving, we use a producer-consumer pattern using Python queues:.

The producer thread packs batches and puts them in a queue, while the main thread pulls them out as needed. This overlap keeps the pipeline flowing smoothly.

First, we try a simple greedy packing strategy:.

According to recent reports, this walks through the data sequentially, adding items to a pack until it’s full, then starting a fresh one. It’s fast but not perfect. Here’s what the batches look like:.

Notice how later batches get sparse? We’re leaving gaps.

Let’s try a smarter approach: bin-packing (specifically, First Fit Decreasing):.

Recent findings suggest that this sorts sequences by length (longest first) and tries to fit each one into the first pack that has room. If none fits, it starts a upcoming pack. The result?

According to recent reports, these batches are much tighter, with less wasted space. It’s like playing Tetris with your data, fitting pieces together snugly.

Now for the real deal, applying knapsack packing to our multimodal dataset.

We’re back to images, prompts, and responses, and we need to pack them efficiently while respecting both token limits and image budgets. Image budgeting is done so that images per sample are balanced. We would like to avoid the case where one GPU needs to process way more images than another.

In a recent development, our newly introduced ConstantLengthDataset class handles the heavy lifting. Here’s how it works, compared to Stage 4:.

The ConstantLengthDataset does it all:.

Look at that! The gray (padding) is minimal, and the batches are dense with useful data. It’s like packing a suitcase so well you can still zip it up without sitting on it.

The image might seem unintuive at the first glance, but let us look at the image side by side with constrained padding.

Here you will notice that the samples in knapsack are more evenly distributed. We also do not run into the problem of having less samples in the batch due to filtering.

What started as a simple "why is training so slow?" investigation led to a complete rethink of how we handle multimodal data.

The balanced knapsack strategy for data pipeline comes from the Eagle 2: Building Post-Training Data Strategies from Scratch for Frontier Vision-Language Models paper from NVIDIA.

Happy training (and may your GPUs stay busy)!

According to recent reports, there’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

For Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other notable parts of your digital life — organized.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

It has been revealed that unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

It has been revealed that proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

According to recent reports, an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

If that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

According to recent reports, proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

When you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

In a recent development, pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

According to recent reports, pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

According to recent reports, proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to new consumers and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Industry observers note that not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

Sources indicate that this guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and looks, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

It has been revealed that openArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

In a recent development, the direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt says Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: Fresh accounts get 40 free credits. Paid plans add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

ElevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free strategy includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid looks start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

Recent findings suggest that pricing: Free proposal with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

It has been revealed that murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

According to recent reports, pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Sources indicate that newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

Recent findings suggest that the say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

In a recent development, what is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. In a recent development, can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

How do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

According to recent reports, AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. Latest Update: Three Mighty Alerts Supporting Hugging Face’s Production Infrastructure
