💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, loRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes.
  • It has been revealed that in this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x).
  • Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, loRA adapters provide a great deal of customization for models of all shapes and sizes. When it comes to image generation, they can empower the models with different styles, different characters, and much more. Sometimes, they can also be leveraged to reduce inference latency. Hence, their importance is paramount, particularly when it comes to customizing and fine-tuning models.

It has been revealed that in this post, we take the Flux.1-Dev model for text-to-image generation because of its widespread popularity and adoption, and how to optimize its inference speed when using LoRAs (~2.3x). It has over 30k adapters trained with it (as reported on the Hugging Face Hub platform). Therefore, its importance to the community is significant.

Note that even though we demonstrate speedups with Flux, our belief is that our recipe is generic enough to be applied to other models as well.

If you cannot wait to get started with the code, please check out the accompanying code repository.

When serving LoRAs, it is common to hotswap (swap in and swap out different LoRAs) them. A LoRA changes the base model architecture. Additionally, LoRAs can be different from one another – each one of them could have varying ranks and different layers they target for adaptation. To account for these dynamic properties of LoRAs, we must take necessary steps to ensure the optimizations we apply are robust.

Sources indicate that for example, we can apply torch.compile on a model loaded with a particular LoRA to obtain speedups on inference latency. However, the moment we swap out the LoRA with a different one (with a potentially different configuration), we will run into recompilation complications, causing slowdowns in inference.

According to recent reports, one can also fuse the LoRA parameters into the base model parameters, run compilation, and unfuse the LoRA parameters when loading upcoming ones. However, this approach will again encounter the problem of recompilation whenever inference is run, due to potential architecture-level changes.

Our optimization recipe takes into account the above-mentioned situations to be as realistic as possible. Below are the key components of our optimization recipe:.

Industry observers note that note that amongst the above-mentioned, FP8 quantization is lossy but often provides the most formidable speed-memory trade-off. Even though we tested the recipe primarily using NVIDIA GPUs, it should work on AMD GPUs, too.

Sources indicate that in our previous blog posts (post 1 and post 2), we have already discussed the benefits of using the first three components of our optimization recipe. Applying them one by one is just a few lines of code:.

The FA3 processor comes from here.

The problems start surfacing when we try to swap in and swap out LoRAs into a compiled diffusion transformer (pipe.transformer) without triggering recompilation.

According to recent reports, normally, loading and unloading LoRAs will require recompilation, which defeats any speed advantage gained from compilation. Thankfully, there is a way to avoid the need for recompilation. By passing hotswap=True, diffusers will leave the model architecture unchanged and only exchange the weights of the LoRA adapter itself, which does not necessitate recompilation.

(As a reminder, the first call to pipe will be slow as torch.compile is a just-in-time compiler. However, the subsequent calls should be significantly faster.).

This generally allows for swapping LoRAs without recompilation, but there are limitations:.

For more information on hotswapping in Diffusers and its limitations, visit the hotswapping section of the documentation.

The benefits of this workflow become evident when we look at the inference latency without using compilation with hotswapping.

The optimization recipe we have discussed so far assumes access to a powerful GPU like H100. However, what can we do when we’re limited to using consumer GPUs such as RTX 4090? Let’s find out.

Recent findings suggest that flux.1-Dev (without any LoRA), using the Bfloat16 data-type, takes ~33GB of memory to run. Depending on the size of the LoRA module, and without using any optimization, this memory footprint can increase even further. Many consumer GPUs like the RTX 4090 only have 24GB. Throughout the rest of this section, we will consider an RTX 4090 machine as our testbed.

According to recent reports, first, to enable end-to-end execution of Flux.1-Dev, we can apply CPU offloading wherein components that are not needed to execute the current computation are offloaded to the CPU to free more accelerator memory. Doing so allows us to run the entire pipeline in ~22GB in 35.403 seconds on an RTX 4090. Enabling compilation can reduce the latency down to 31.205 seconds (1.12x speedup). In terms of code, it’s just a few lines:.

Notice that we didn’t apply the FP8 quantization here because it’s not supported with CPU offloading and compilation (supporting issue thread). Therefore, just applying FP8 quantization to the Flux Transformer isn’t enough to mitigate the memory exhaustion problem, either. In this instance, we decided to remove it.

Therefore, to take advantage of the FP8 quantization scheme, we need to find a way to do it without CPU offloading. For Flux.1-Dev, if we additionally apply quantization to the T5 text encoder, we should be able to load and run the complete pipeline in 24GB. Below is a comparison of the results with and without the T5 text encoder being quantized (NF4 quantization from bitsandbytes).

As we can notice in the figure above, quantizing the T5 text encoder doesn’t incur too much of a quality loss. Combining the quantized T5 text encoder and FP8-quantized Flux Transformer with torch.compile gives us somewhat reasonable results – 9.668 seconds from 32.27 seconds (a massive ~3.3x speedup) without a noticeable quality drop.

It is possible to generate images with 24 GB of VRAM even without quantizing the T5 text encoder, but that would have made our generation pipeline slightly more complicated.

Sources indicate that we now have a way to run the entire Flux.1-Dev pipeline with FP8 quantization on an RTX 4090. We can apply the previously established optimization recipe for optimizing LoRA inference on the same hardware. Since FA3 isn’t supported on RTX 4090, we will stick to the following optimization recipe with T5 quantization newly added to the mix:.

In the table below, we show the inference latency numbers with different combinations of the above components applied.

Recent findings suggest that to enable hotswapping without triggering recompilation, two hurdles have to be overcome. First, the LoRA scaling factor has to be converted into torch tensors from floats, which is achieved fairly easily. Second, the shape of the LoRA weights needs to padded to the largest required shape. That way, the data in the weights can be replaced without the need to reassign the whole attribute. This is why the max_rank argument discussed above is crucial. As we pad the values with zeros, the results remain unchanged, although the computation is slowed down a bit depending on how large the padding is.

Recent findings suggest that since no new LoRA attributes are added, this also requires that each LoRA after the first one can only target the same layers, or a subset of layers, that the first one targets. Thus, choose the order of loading wisely. If LoRAs target disjoint layers, there is the possibility to create a dummy LoRA that targets the union of all target layers.

To see the nitty-gritty of this implementation, visit the hotswap.py file in PEFT.

According to recent reports, this post outlined an optimization recipe for fast LoRA inference with Flux, demonstrating significant speedups. Our approach combines Flash Attention 3, torch.compile, and FP8 quantization while ensuring hotswapping capabilities without recompilation problems. On high-end GPUs like the H100, this optimized setup provides a 2.23x speedup over the baseline.

For consumer GPUs, specifically the RTX 4090, we tackled memory limitations by introducing T5 text encoder quantization (NF4) and leveraging regional compilation. This comprehensive recipe achieved a substantial 2.04x speedup, making LoRA inference on Flux viable and performant even with limited VRAM. The key insight is that by carefully managing compilation and quantization, the benefits of LoRA can be fully realized across different hardware configurations.

Hopefully, the recipes from this post will inspire you to optimize your LoRA-based use cases, benefitting from speedy inference.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself.
  • In a recent development, but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Docker is officially launching its latest brand, and I’m excited to tell you what it’s all about and why we think now is the time for change.

Let’s start with the big picture. We’re living through a transformative moment: for Docker, for developers, for the industry, and quite possibly, for humanity itself. AI is creating possibilities that would have sounded like science fiction not long ago.

In a recent development, but it’s also forcing the industry to confront an almost existential question: how do we harness all that power and intelligence without compromising security, governance, or control? Or, put more simply: how do we get to a point where we can actually trust agents?

That one seemingly simple yet infinitely complex question is why we’re here today, introducing you to a latest Docker.

A fresh Docker, but a familiar story.

Ok, not exactly here, but once upon a time, a decade or so ago, the tech industry was at a similar inflection point. Digital transformation was the term du jour, promising a latest way of engaging customers and powering the global economy. There was one big constraint, though: teams needed a better way to build, ship, and run software consistently across any environment.

Enter a organization you might have heard of: Docker.

According to recent reports, together with all of you, Docker built the standard trusted by millions of developers. For over a decade, developers have relied on us to make software portable, open, reproducible, and secure. Docker turned the frustration of “Well, it works on my machine!” into the assurance that “Yes, it works everywhere.”.

It has been revealed that today, of course, the challenge confronting us is new and evolving, and we all need to evolve with it. We cannot simply continue to do what we’ve always done and expect to succeed in this new era. That applies to business leaders, developers, tech companies, everyone. It certainly applies to Docker. That’s what this rebrand is about: evolving to meet the moment for our customers.

Let me be unequivocal: this is not about leaving Docker’s legacy or heritage behind. We’ve spent more than a decade earning your trust. This is about building on that foundation, not replacing it.

Sources indicate that the qualities you value us for aren’t changing. We’re still committed to openness and industry collaboration. We’re still, and always will be, developer-first. We’re still fanatical about simplicity, and about showing up everywhere you need us.

On the product front, the containers you know and love aren’t going anywhere. Containers still play a huge role in the software development lifecycle. As long as that’s the case, Docker will continue leading the way.

Recent findings suggest that agents have introduced a new problem. Containers isolate workloads. But agents aren’t workloads. Agents are actors.

Agents make their own decisions about what to run, what to access, and what to change. Developers and enterprises need solutions built specifically to isolate and govern them, so they can give those agents real autonomy without giving up control.

Docker’s next chapter is about delivering exactly that: security, isolation, and governance, so we can all trust agents to do meaningful work without feeling like we’re always one step from catastrophe.

In case I haven’t made it blindingly obvious yet, the new Docker is all about trust.

Trust Docker because our track record speaks for itself. Trust Docker because we’re proven, neutral, and secure. Trust Docker because it’s pretty darn clear you can’t trust the agents to manage themselves.

In a recent development, trust us because we have a software supply chain that is already the standard for building securely. Trust us because nobody isolates agents where they run better than we do. Trust us because we’re taking a comprehensive approach to improving governance and minimizing risk across the entire enterprise.

Trust Docker because we’re not egotistical enough to think we can solve a challenge this big alone. Trust us because everything about our history, our heritage, and our actions over the past year tells you we’ll partner with the smartest and build alongside the best, and not create vendor lock-in.

Most of all, trust Docker because we’re not just talking the talk. We’ve got the goods to back it up: trusted supply chain for your agents to build from, trusted runtime to isolate your agents, and a trusted ecosystem to ensure all the layers of trust are covered, whether made by Docker or not.

As our product team innovated to meet the moment and our messaging in the market began to shift, one thing became clear: the speed and scale of evolution happening inside Docker called for an equally momentous evolution on the outside. Something that makes it unmistakably clear that it’s a new day for Docker. Something that indicates and reveals, loud and clear, for all the world to see, that Docker is not just about containers anymore.

Something, dare I say, whale sized.

I’m talking, of course, about our beloved Moby.

In a recent development, if you know Docker, then you know Moby, and if Docker is evolving, Moby should too. The only question was to how and to what extent? We looked at a lot of whales, folks. (I may or may not have been seeing whales in my sleep.) Ultimately, with the help of our friends at the strategic brand transformation company, Motto, we landed on a fresh Moby for the new Docker.

Watch Moby’s transformation here:.

In many ways, Moby is a microcosm for Docker and the changes we’re making: the Moby you love and trust, evolved for a upcoming era. Just as the new Docker is no longer singularly defined by containers, neither is the new Moby.

We’ve got lots to show you. Poke around our newly introduced website. Find and engage with the new Docker brand on social media. And if you want to see what trust in the agentic era looks like in practice, try Docker Sandboxes and Docker AI Governance. We’d love to hear what you think.

Recent findings suggest that wherever this new era takes us, Docker will always honor and cherish the trust you continue to place in us. Now, let’s go build what’s next.

Chief Marketing Officer, Docker.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

DoJ claims suspect part of 4-month operation to steal secrets, surveil employees.

A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech manufacturer in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes.

Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent.

After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company.

Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war.

While unconfirmed officially, the firm has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation.

D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July.

The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the organization’s employees.

In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device.

The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims.

D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so.

One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong.

D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots.

The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler.

Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but  claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date.

The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations.

In a recent development, according to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 demonstrated that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US.

Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram.

A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp.

The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico.

Records obtained from Google revealed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the tech giant's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints.

The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers.

Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing.

Recent findings suggest that D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash.

The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco.

The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed firm's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed.

Industry observers note that contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else.

It has been revealed that the affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept.

These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a Fresh York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns.".

He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing.

One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there.

FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being:.

A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for manufacturer employees’ homes.

Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses.

Per the affidavit, D'iu was mentioned to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex.

"D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated.

At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the firm he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government.

Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources.

"D'iu's targeting of the organization and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine.".

Sources indicate that the Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®.

Latest Update: TimeScope: How Long Can Your Video Large Multimodal Model Go?

📅 23 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1015 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TimeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos.
  • Recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos.
  • Text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TimeScope is an open-source benchmark designed to measure how well vision-language models understand long videos. By adding short “needle” clips into videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours, it evaluates three skills:.

Recent advances in multimodal AI have produced models claiming to understand hour-long videos. This trend mirrors progress in long-context language models, which excel at reasoning over lengthy text. Following this, vision-language systems now advertise context windows that can handle thousands of frames. But these claims require a closer look: do these models truly demonstrate understanding of the sequence of events? Are they limited to surface-level retrieval \ recognition? It's crucial to ask if their capabilities are being overstated.

Text benchmarks such as HELM and RULER have exposed the fragility of long-context claims, showing that models often struggle when tasks demand more than simple retrieval, like reasoning or aggregation at long context lengths. In the video domain, however, we're still playing catch-up. The most common test, Video Needle in a Haystack (VideoNIAH), injects static images as "needles" into videos, effectively measuring visual search rather than true temporal dynamics. As a result, even top-tier models advertising massive frame capacities are rarely trained beyond ~256 frames and see sharp drops on benchmarks like Video-MME when pushed further.

This measurement gap leaves us wondering: What does it really mean for a model to "understand" long videos? To address this, we're excited to introduce TimeScope, a new open-source benchmark hosted on Hugging Face. TimeScope probes the limits of long-video capabilities by inserting several short (~5-10 second) video clips—our "needles"—into base videos ranging from 1 minute to 8 hours. With three distinct task types, it evaluates not just retrieval but synthesis, localization, and fine-grained motion analysis, providing a more holistic view of temporal comprehension.

Sources indicate that the promise of long-video AI is transformative — enabling agents to summarize hours of footage, detect subtle anomalies, and answer complex questions about extended narratives. Integrated into robotics, these models could analyze prolonged operations, adapt in real time, and push autonomous decision-making. Just as powerful is the vision of a personal assistant that understands daily life and offers continuous, actionable feedback.

In practice, this leads to overstated capabilities. Models might claim to process 10,000+ frames, but training data often caps at 256 frames per clip, leading to degraded performance on longer inputs. We've seen this in evaluations where increasing frame sampling rates tanks accuracy on tasks requiring temporal insight.

TimeScope flips the script by emphasizing three pillars of long-video understanding:.

Sources indicate that timeScope’s key idea is using short video clips as “needles,” and instead of just spotting the needle, it pushes models to deeply understand the whole video. We start with a long base video (e.g., a documentary, lecture, or ambient footage) and insert one or more hand-curated short video needles (5-10 seconds each) at random positions. These needles contain the key information needed to solve the task, forcing models to process the entire input without shortcuts like sparse sampling.

It has been revealed that figure 1: Overview of TimeScope's needle insertion process. A long base video (1 min to 8 hours) serves as the haystack, into which we splice short video needles (~5-10 seconds). Tasks require detecting, synthesizing, or analyzing content from these needles, embedded at varying depths.

We evaluate across three needle types, each targeting a different aspect of long-video comprehension:.

Recent findings suggest that this tests basic retrieval and understanding of a localized event. Questions are put so that sampling a relevant frame from the needle should suffice—like asking about a shorter part in a longer video.

Example:What mode of transportation is shown in the video?

Here, we embed multiple text-based needles (e.g., 2-4 short clips displaying "secret words" via on-screen text) at different points in the video. The model must identify all words and report them in chronological order, simulating tasks like extracting timestamps or key facts from dispersed scenes. This requires scanning the full timeline and understanding relative positioning.

It has been revealed that for questions focusing on motion or sequences within a short clip, single-frame sampling won't cut it—the model needs to perceive dynamics across frames. This probes whether long-context handling preserves temporal fidelity.

Example:How many times did the man swing his axe? (a) one (b) two (c) three (d) four (e) five (f) six.

With different video lengths and varying needle placements, TimeScope measures how much video a model can really handle—and shows that performance drops as the video gets longer.

To kick things off, we ran TimeScope on a suite of leading vision-language models, from open-source favorites to the juggernauts like Gemini 2.5-Pro. The results underscore the benchmark’s value: even models that claim to handle long videos well still struggle with real long-video tasks. These findings reveal clear patterns—performance cliffs around certain durations, strengths in static retrieval versus weaknesses in motion analysis—and pave the way for targeted improvements in model training. For detailed results and visualizations, check out our Hugging Face Space embedded above.

Recent findings suggest that model size isn’t everything. Qwen 2.5-VL 3B and 7B, as well as InternVL 2.5 models at 2B, 4B, and 8B parameters, exhibit nearly indistinguishable long-video curves to their smaller counterparts. All of them plateau at roughly the same context length, showing that simply scaling parameters does not automatically grant a longer temporal horizon.

Sources indicate that gemini 2.5-Pro is in a league of its own. It is the only model that maintains strong accuracy on videos longer than one hour.

Trade-offs across tasks matter. Qwen 2.5-VL shines in the Information-Synthesis (OCR) task—identifying and ordering dispersed text snippets—yet it falls behind on Fine-Grained Temporal Perception, where precise motion counting is required.

In a recent development, timeScope demonstrates that “hour-long video understanding” is still more slogan than reality. By revealing where even state-of-the-art models stumble on temporal reasoning, information synthesis, and motion perception, the benchmark invites us to rethink how we train and evaluate multimodal systems.

We hope this benchmark helps the community make steady, measurable progress toward models that better understand video over time.

We are open-sourcing all components of TimeScope:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenJDK and Oracle disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) on November 17, and NGINX released fixes for two HTTP/2 flaws the next day. Docker began publishing fixed images for both in the Docker Hardened Images (DHI) catalog starting that same day.

What we know about Java4Shell is that it’s a memory-corruption bug in the Java runtime that can let an attacker with no credentials run code inside a Java application. Many container images contain a Java runtime, including application images that bundle their own, so it affects teams well beyond the ones that write Java.

Recent findings suggest that docker Hardened Images are the trusted foundation your applications should run on, because a flaw in the runtime inside an image is fixed only when that image is rebuilt, and Docker rebuilds its hardened images as soon as upstream fixes become available. Fixed images for the Amazon Corretto, SapMachine and Azul Zulu runtimes and for NGINX are in the catalog today, with Eclipse Temurin following as soon as Adoptium completes its fixed builds.

To decode Base64 swiftly, the HotSpot JVM uses a hand-written routine built on AVX-512 instructions. That routine miscalculates a length when the input ends in unexpected padding and writes up to 62 bytes past the end of a buffer on the Java heap. Calif, the researchers who found it, turned that into heap disclosure and remote code execution.

It has been revealed that they demonstrated code execution before authentication against default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and after authentication against Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. They note there is no universal exploit: each application needs its own, and they have not published those. As of November 18 there are no public reports of exploitation in the wild.

Sources indicate that oracle rates the issue 8.1 (High) under CVSS 3.1. The researchers rate it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0. CISA has issued an alert urging immediate patching.

All three of these must be true.

Sources indicate that to check a host’s CPU, run this on the host or Kubernetes node. Hardened runtime images have no shell, so it will not run inside the container.

grep -m1 ‘^flags’ /proc/cpuinfo | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep -E ‘^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$’.

The host is affected if all four flags are printed.

Two other ways to check, for when a shell on the node is hard to get.

Ask the JVM. This works in hardened images:.

docker run –rm –entrypoint java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep -w UseAVX.

Industry observers note that useAVX = 3 means the JVM is using AVX-512 on that host. Treat the host as affected until the full check states otherwise. A value of 0 to 2 means AVX-512 is not in use. On ARM64 nothing is printed. The answer applies only to the host the command ran on.

Ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type shows the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Check build runners and CI workers as well. They run Java, and they talk to the network.

Industry observers note that ask Kubernetes. kubectl get nodes -L kubernetes.io/arch,node.kubernetes.io/instance-type demonstrates the architecture and instance type of every node. If you run Node Feature Discovery, nodes with the instruction set carry the label feature.node.kubernetes.io/cpu-cpuid.AVX512VBMI=true.

Fixed. The published images report 17.0.21.1.2, 21.0.13.1.2, 25.0.5.1.2 and 27.0.1.1.4.

Fixed. The published images report 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

Industry observers note that fixed. The published Zulu images we checked report 17.0.21.1+2, 21.0.13.1+2, 25.0.5.1+2 and 27.0.1.1+4.

In a recent development, waiting for Adoptium to complete its release. On November 18 Adoptium had published 27.0.1.1+4 for x86-64 Linux only. 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1 and 25.0.5.1 were still in testing. Java 26 reached end of support in September 2026, so no fix is expected from any vendor, and it is not among the fixed lines in the OpenJDK advisory. If you run it, treat it as affected and keep the flag set. We recommend moving to Java 25 or updating to Java 27. If you cannot migrate yet, ask us whether Extended Lifecycle Support can cover your version. It is the Docker Hardened Images Enterprise add-on for software past its upstream end of life.

Not affected by this CVE and no action is needed for it. The same November revision fixes other issues in these lines, so update when new images arrive.

Application images that bundle Java, such as Keycloak, Jenkins, Kafka, Elasticsearch and Solr.

They follow the bundled runtime, which for many of them is Temurin, and they are rebuilt once the runtime they use is fixed. Until then, set the flag yourself.

It has been revealed that set the mitigation flag yourself on every JVM that is still waiting for a fixed runtime, and check what each image already sets before you do. Treat the flag as a stopgap, because a JVM is protected only if the flag reaches it when it starts, and a deployment setting or a start script can override it or drop it. A fixed runtime is the only thing that closes the problem, so move to the fixed image as soon as it is published.

The CPU check and the mitigation flag in the steps below apply to any image that runs a HotSpot-based OpenJDK build. The version strings in this post come from Docker Hardened Images, so for an image from another source, confirm the fixed build in that source’s advisory.

The fixed build can only come from whoever builds your image, because the Java runtime and the system packages your application runs on come from the image underneath it. That dependency is why a hardened image is a necessary step toward a trusted software supply chain. With Docker Hardened Images, tracking each vendor’s fix and rebuilding on it is work Docker does for you. The images are minimal and secure by default, and they are built to serve as a trusted and verifiable upstream for your builds. You can move a service onto one by following the migration guide.

A container often runs more than one JVM, for example when a build tool forks a JVM for tests, an application server starts helper processes or a CI agent starts a JVM for every build step. The flag protects only the JVMs that receive it, and the variable most people reach for first is JAVA_OPTS, which Java does not read at all.

The JVM itself, however it is started. Includes javac, keytool and other JDK tools.

Yes, through the inherited environment.

Industry observers note that A Java 8 JVM that sees it refuses to start. Some DHI FIPS images already set this variable.

Only the java launcher, Java 9 and later.

Yes, when the child is started with java.

Not read by javac, keytool or other JDK tools. DHI FIPS images set it. Java 8 ignores it.

Nothing downstream inherits it.

JAVA_OPTS, JENKINS_JAVA_OPTS, MAVEN_OPTS, ES_JAVA_OPTS and similar.

A start script, which copies the value onto one java command line.

According to recent reports, each script has its own rules. If nothing in the image reads the variable, it does nothing.

According to recent reports, five rules follow from that table. We tested each on DHI images.

JAVA_OPTS only works where a script reads it. With JAVA_OPTS=”-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics” set and a plain java command, the intrinsic stays on. No warning is printed.

Recent findings suggest that A flag on the command line stops at that process. We started a JVM with the flag on its command line and had it start a second JVM. The child ran with the intrinsic on. With JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS in the environment, the child ran with it off. A child started with a cleared environment gets nothing, whichever variable you use.

Recent findings suggest that check what the image already sets before you set anything. In Docker and Kubernetes, your value replaces the image’s value. It is not appended.

docker inspect –format ‘{{range .Config.Env}}{{println .}}{{end}}’ \  | grep -E ‘^(JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS|JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS)=’.

According to recent reports, our FIPS images use these variables to configure the FIPS provider. dhi.io/eclipse-temurin:21-fips sets both. When we replaced its JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS with only the flag, the JVM started normally, but the org.bouncycastle.fips.approved_only property was gone. Nothing warned us. If the command prints a value, copy it and add the flag at the end:.

env:  – name: JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS    value: “ -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics”.

Not every FIPS image uses the same variables, so run the check for each image.

Recent findings suggest that keep JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS away from Java 8. Java 8 is not affected and does not know the flag:.

Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS: -XX:-UseBASE64IntrinsicsUnrecognized VM option ‘UseBASE64Intrinsics’Error: Could not create the Java Virtual Machine.

Recent findings suggest that adding -XX:+IgnoreUnrecognizedVMOptions to the variable does not help on Java 8. Where Java 8 shares an environment with a newer Java, either scope the variable to the containers that need it or use JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS, which Java 8 ignores. Java 11 accepts the flag, so it is harmless there.

In a recent development, verify the process, not the environment. Running java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version inside a container starts a new JVM. It tells you what the environment gives a new JVM, not what the JVM already serving traffic was started with. For the running process, use the startup log line. JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS prints one too, starting with NOTE: Picked up. In an image that includes the JDK you can also ask the process directly:.

jcmd VM.flags | tr ‘ ‘ ‘\n’ | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.

According to recent reports, the answer must be -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. If the flag reached the JVM through an environment variable, it will not show in the process’s command line, so ps is not a reliable check.

Some applications discard these variables on purpose. Elasticsearch’s start script, for example, ignores JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS and expects ES_JAVA_OPTS. Check your application’s documentation.

Pull the newly introduced image and redeploy. Four things catch people out:.

Then confirm with java -version that what is running reports a fixed build. After that, remove the flag from every place you set it.

The day after Java4Shell, NGINX released fixes for two memory errors in the way it handles HTTP/2 connections, tracked as CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. A crafted request can crash a worker process, and where an attacker gets past the operating system’s memory protections it can run code inside that worker. Both flaws need HTTP/2 to be enabled on the server, and the same releases fix other NGINX challenges that do not depend on HTTP/2, so upgrade either way.

The Docker Hardened Images for NGINX were rebuilt on NGINX 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and published on November 18, the same day as the upstream release. To patch, pull the image again and redeploy, and move any tag pinned to an older exact version to a fixed one. nginx -v prints the version, and the fixed ones are 1.30.7 and 1.31.9. The notes on pull policy, mirrors and your own images in the section above apply to NGINX images in the same way.

The vulnerable code is in the Java runtime inside the image, and if you are using DHI, shipping the fix becomes our job. Whether that code can be reached in your deployment depends on things an image cannot see: the CPU it is scheduled onto, the options you start it with, the processes it starts, and the traffic you send it.

With Docker Hardened Images, Docker will.

Three jobs stay with you whichever image you run.

It has been revealed that it was only four weeks ago that the news was PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Calif, the security research team that found Java4Shell and helped find PHP2Shell, indicates it used AI to find this flaw in about an hour and that the whole effort cost less than $200 in tokens. When a flaw like this can be found and weaponized at that price, it is reasonable to expect more of them.

Sources indicate that if you lead a team or answer for how your organization builds and ships software, the questions after a week like this one are whether you were exposed and how promptly you can prove you were not. It is imperative to have a trusted foundation in place before the next flaw appears, and Docker Hardened Images is that foundation to adopt. This week Docker began publishing fixed Java and NGINX images to the catalog within a day of each disclosure, with the images still waiting listed in the status table above. Each image ships with a signed SBOM and SLSA Build Level 3 provenance, so you have a record of what it contains and how it was built.

In a recent development, the Docker Hardened Images catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, and moving one of your services onto a hardened image typically means changing one line in its Dockerfile. If you are not building on Docker Hardened Images yet, start today.

TrendForce sees supply outpacing demand in 2027, though cheaper flash won't fix the DRAM squeeze.

NAND flash prices could start falling next year as Chinese cloud operators cut enterprise SSD orders, helping push the market toward oversupply.

Taiwan-based market intelligence firm TrendForce says Chinese cloud service providers are grappling with GPU shortages, high inventories, and fierce competition over AI token pricing.

According to recent reports, as a result, they have reduced their total enterprise SSD orders for 2027 by a substantial amount. Although TrendForce doesn't specify any figures, it says the cutbacks in China are large enough to outweigh the additional demand coming from US-based cloud operators.

But don't get too excited: TrendForce forecasts overall NAND flash contract prices falling by 0-5 percent quarter on quarter in early 2027, with all product categories entering a downturn from the second quarter.

Sources indicate that falling orders are only half the story. Manufacturers are also increasing output, while weaker consumer electronics sales could further depress demand.

In a recent development, strong demand for high-performance storage in the US continues to drive manufacturers to expand capacity and upgrade to newer process technologies. At the same time, the rising adoption of quad-level cell (QLC) technology and increasing number of layers in the NAND chips will further boost bit output, TrendForce observes.

Some suppliers may go slower on their expansion plans in response to sluggish consumer demand, but the firm still expects global NAND flash output, measured in storage capacity, to grow by 25 to 30 percent in 2027.

US restrictions on access to advanced AI chips could put Chinese cloud operators under further pressure. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has introduced new restrictions on sales of GPUs, and on remote access to them via the cloud.

The upcoming restrictions "set everyone back in China," as The Register reported.

TrendForce adds the caveat to its forecast that its market outlook depends on factors such as the pace of inventory reduction among Chinese CSPs, further changes to the restrictions on overseas GPU procurement, and whether device makers continue reducing storage capacities in 2028.

According to recent reports, sadly, cheaper NAND wouldn't resolve the separate squeeze on DRAM supplies. The situation, caused by memory makers opting to produce high-margin products for the AI market rather than mainstream chips, has already increased prices of PCs in Europe by double-digit percentages, leading to a fall in shipments as buyers balk at the cost. ®.

Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (569 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

To scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

To address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

The Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This problem is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

It has been revealed that in multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Recent findings suggest that within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

In a recent development, using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the latest Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.
  • Industry observers note that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.
  • Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reduce Parquet file upload and download times on Hugging Face Hub by leveraging the latest Xet storage layer and Apache Arrow’s Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) feature enabling more efficient and scalable data workflows.

Industry observers note that TL;DR: Parquet Content-Defined Chunking (CDC) is now available in PyArrow and Pandas, enabling efficient deduplication of Parquet files on content-addressable storage systems like Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. CDC dramatically reduces data transfer and storage costs by uploading or downloading only the changed data chunks. Enable CDC by passing the use_content_defined_chunking argument:.

Apache Parquet is a columnar storage format that is widely used in the data engineering community.

As of today, Hugging Face hosts nearly 21 PB of datasets, with Parquet files alone accounting for over 4 PB of that storage. Optimizing Parquet storage is therefore a high priority. Hugging Face has introduced a fresh storage layer called Xet that leverages content-defined chunking to efficiently deduplicate chunks of data reducing storage costs and improving download/upload speeds.

While Xet is format agnostic, Parquet's layout and column-chunk (data page) based compression can produce entirely different byte-level representations for data with minor changes, leading to suboptimal deduplication performance. To address this, the Parquet files should be written in a way that minimizes the byte-level differences between similar data, which is where content-defined chunking (CDC) comes into play.

Let's explore the performance benefits of the new Parquet CDC feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer.

For demonstration purposes, we will use a manageable sized subset of OpenOrca dataset.

Since pyarrow>=21.0.0 we can use Hugging Face URIs in the pyarrow functions to directly read and write parquet (and other file formats) files to the Hub using the hf:// URI scheme.

In a recent development, we can see that the table has been uploaded entirely (total bytes == total transfer) as new data because it is not known to the Xet storage layer yet. Now read it back as a pyarrow table:.

Note that all pyarrow functions that accept a file path also accept a Hugging Face URI, like pyarrow datasets, CSV functions, incremental Parquet writer or reading only the parquet metadata:.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of the content-defined chunking feature, we will try out how it performs in case of:.

While this use case sounds trivial, traditional file systems do not deduplicate files resulting in full re-upload and re-download of the data. In contrast, a system utilizing content-defined chunking can recognize that the file content is identical and avoid unnecessary data transfer.

Recent findings suggest that we can see that no new data has been uploaded, and the operation was instantaneous. Now let's see what happens if we upload the same file again but to a different repository:.

According to recent reports, the upload was instantaneous again since deduplication works across repositories as well. This is a key feature of the Xet storage layer, allowing efficient data sharing and collaboration. You can read more about the details and scaling challenges in the From Chunks to Blocks: Accelerating Uploads and Downloads on the Hub blog post.

First write out the original and changed tables to local parquet files to see their sizes:.

Now upload them to Hugging Face to see how much data is actually transferred:.

We can see that only the new columns and the new parquet metadata placed in the file's footer were uploaded, while the original data was not transferred again. This is a huge benefit of the Xet storage layer, as it allows us to efficiently add new columns without transferring the entire dataset again.

Same applies to removing columns, as we can see below:.

To have a better understanding of what has been uploaded, we can visualize the differences between the two parquet files using the deduplication estimation tool:.

Adding two latest columns mean that we have unseen data pages which must be transferred (highlighted in red), but the rest of the data remains unchanged (highlighted in green), so it is not transferred again. Note the small red area in the footer metadata which almost always changes as we modify the parquet file. The dedup stats show / = where smaller ratios mean higher deduplication performance.

Also visualize the difference after removing a column:.

Since we are removing entire columns we can only see changes in the footer metadata, all the other columns remain unchanged and already existing in the storage layer, so they are not transferred again.

Another common use case is changing the column types in the table e.g. to reduce the storage size or to optimize the data for specific queries. Let's change the question_length column from int64 data type to int32 and see how much data is transferred:.

It has been revealed that again, we can see that only the newly introduced column and the updated parquet metadata were uploaded. Now visualize the deduplication heatmap:.

In a recent development, the first red region indicates the newly introduced column that was added, while the second red region indicates the updated metadata in the footer. The rest of the data remains unchanged and is not transferred again.

We are going to append latest rows by concatenating another slice of the original dataset to the table.

Now check that only the new rows are being uploaded since the original data is already known to the Xet storage layer:.

Since each column gets newly introduced data, we can see multiple red regions. This is due to the actual parquet file specification where whole columns are laid out after each other (within each row group).

It has been revealed that here comes the difficult part as insertions and deletions are shifting the existing rows which lead to different columns chunks or data pages in the parquet nomenclature. Since each data page is compressed separately, even a single row insertion or deletion can lead to a completely different byte-level representation starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

This parquet specific problem cannot be solved by the Xet storage layer alone, the parquet file itself needs to be written in a way that minimizes the data page differences even if there are inserted or deleted rows.

Let's try to use the existing mechanism and see how it performs.

Also visualize both cases to see the differences:.

We can see that the deduplication performance has dropped significantly (higher ratio), and the deduplication heatmaps show that the compressed parquet files are quite different from each other. This is due to the fact that the inserted and deleted rows have shifted the existing rows, leading to different data pages starting from the edited row(s) to the end of the parquet file.

We can solve this problem by writing parquet files with a latest pyarrow feature called content-defined chunking (CDC). This feature ensures that the columns are consistently getting chunked into data pages based on their content, similarly how the Xet storage layer deduplicates data but applied to the logical values of the columns before any serialization or compression happens.

The feature can be enabled by passing use_content_defined_chunking=True to the write_parquet function:.

Pandas also supports the upcoming feature:.

Let's visualize the deduplication difference before and after using the Parquet CDC feature:.

In a recent development, looks much better! Since the proof of the pudding is in the eating, let's actually upload the tables using the content-defined chunking parquet feature and see how much data is transferred.

Note that we need to upload the original table first with content-defined chunking enabled:.

The uploaded data is significantly smaller than before, showing much better deduplication performance as highlighted in the heatmaps above.

Important to note that the same performance benefits apply to downloads using the huggingface_hub.hf_hub_download() and datasets.load_dataset() functions.

There are cases depending on the reader/writer constraints where larger or smaller row-group sizes might be beneficial. The parquet writer implementations use fixed-sized row-groups by default, in the case of pyarrow the default is 1Mi rows. Dataset writers may change to reduce the row-group size in order to improve random access performance or to reduce the memory footprint of the reader application.

Sources indicate that changing the row-group size will shift rows between row-groups, shifting values between data pages, so we have a similar problem as with inserting or deleting rows. Let's compare the deduplication performance between different row-group sizes using the parquet CDC feature:.

According to recent reports, datasets are often split into multiple files to improve parallelism and random access. Parquet CDC combined with the Xet storage layer can efficiently deduplicate data across multiple files even if the data is split at different boundaries.

Let's write out the dataset with three different file-level splitting then compare the deduplication performance:.

Even though we uploaded the dataset with three different sharding configurations, the overall upload size would be barely larger than the original dataset size.

So far we've used PyArrow, let’s explore using the same CDC feature with Pandas by downloading, filtering then uploading the dataset with the content-defined chunking feature enabled:.

In a recent development, since Parquet CDC is applied at the parquet data page level (column chunk level), the deduplication performance depends on the filter's selectivity, or rather the distribution of the changes across the dataset. If most of the data pages are affected, then the deduplication ratio will drop significantly.

More details about the feature can be found at:.

We explored the performance benefits of the latest Parquet content-defined chunking feature used alongside Hugging Face's Xet storage layer. We demonstrated how it can efficiently deduplicate data in various scenarios making parquet operations faster and more storage-efficient. Comparing to traditional cloud storage solutions, the Xet storage layer with Parquet CDC can significantly reduce data transfer times and costs.

Migrate your Hugging Face repositories from Git LFS to Xet to benefit from this here: https://huggingface.co/join/xet.

Does the Hugging Face Xet Storage also work on top of (self-hosted) Minio?

@sfkeller Not today, but the underlying technology is open source and we're in the process of documenting the backend! We plan to release a Xet protocol later this year, which would open up the possibility to build for other backends as well. cc @rajatarya.

This is great! I will look forward to the release of Xet protocol.

I hope it is written in Rust :).

Protocol + Format will be documentation, but there is the hf-xet implementation in Rust with xet-core.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Company still has to contend with massive compute obligations and the threat of open models, neither of which Dario Amodei is worried about, he claims.
  • Welcome to the world of public AI frontier labs: Anthropic is now a publicly-held company with its Thursday IPO, and investors are clamoring for a piece of the pie, for now anyway.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Company still has to contend with massive compute obligations and the threat of open models, neither of which Dario Amodei is worried about, he claims.

Welcome to the world of public AI frontier labs: Anthropic is now a publicly-held company with its Thursday IPO, and investors are clamoring for a piece of the pie, for now anyway.

That $83 IPO price didn’t last long, with shares rocketing to $111.50 by the time the public could get their hands on them at the end of the initial auction. That means that the organization was valued at around $2 trillion as of the public availability of the 980 million shares it put up for sale, a 34 percent increase over the IPO price.

At just under six years old, Anthropic’s meteoric rise to that valuation has sent investors into a frenzy despite uncertainties surrounding the organization’s future profitability. As we’ve noted, Anthropic is on the hook for nearly $1 trillion in compute obligations that could drag its profitability prospects down if any one of a number of scenarios happens to materialize.

Amodei was on hand to address some of those questions with CNBC this morning following the opening of markets on his company’s major day.

When asked about the risk Anthropic’s massive compute bills to its bottom line, Amodei admitted the company’s needs are difficult to predict, and that - get this - they try to err on the low side.

That’s right: The $900 billion in infrastructure and compute commitments that Anthropic revealed in a recent regulatory filing, which could end up surpassing $1T in short order, might just be an underestimate of what the manufacturer will need in coming months and years.

Not to worry, though, the Anthropic CEO insisted: It’s worth it.

“We’re willing to put into place these very large compute spends because, historically, we’ve seen that it pays off,” Amodei told CNBC’s Ross Sorkin, adding that the returns on the cognitive capabilities of its latest models are “so high” as to make all that spending worth it - eventually, one would assume based on his comments, Anthropic is sure to come out on top.

But what of the threat of open models that could undermine the constant push at Anthropic and other frontier labs to create the most power-hungry, resource-intensive, and powerful AI? Bah, that’s not a problem either.

Frontier model makers like Anthropic, Amodei remarked, have already proven that they can do the heavy lifting at the bleeding edge, so you can trust it to make reliable models that are cheaper and less capable, too.

“Anthropic can compete both at and away from the frontier,” The Anthropic CEO said.

Whether that’ll mean long-term success for investors is another thing altogether. Mozilla president Mark Surman doesn’t think valuation translates into long-term success, for one. He told The Register this morning that the one thing he consistently hears from developers is that they want AI they can control, not rent from a frontier lab. As Amodei suggested in his comments, Anthropic is aware that those with less intense AI needs might not choose its models, and that could harm the firm.

“Pushing AI toward open source matters so much right now,” Surman said in an email. “Mozilla’s own research this year found that open source models account for a third of all tokens, while the gap with the best closed models is down to about 3.3 per cent.”.

In other words, keep an eye on that Anthropic stock - it might be hot now, but reality could still catch up to the organization with the biggest-ever IPO.

Industry observers note that “The market is already moving,” Surman said. “No valuation changes that.” ®.

More importantly, the CLI’s command structure became messy as upcoming features were added over time (upload, download, cache management, repo management, etc.). Renaming the CLI is a chance to reorganize commands into a clearer, more consistent format.

We decided not to reinvent the wheel and instead follow a well-known CLI pattern: hf . This predictable grammar makes the Hugging Face CLI more ergonomic and discoverable, while also setting the stage for upcoming features.

To start playing with the latest CLI, you’ll need to install the latest huggingface_hub version:.

It has been revealed that and reload your terminal session. To test the install completed successfully, run hf version:.

Next, let’s explore the new syntax with hf --help:.

Recent findings suggest that as we can see, commands are grouped by "resource" (hf auth, hf cache, hf repo, etc.). We also surface hf upload and hf downloadat the root level since they’re expected to be the most-used commands.

To dive deeper into any command group, simply append --help:.

If you are used to huggingface-cli, most commands will look familiar. The biggest change affects authentication:.

All auth commands have been grouped together with the existing hf auth switch (to switch between different local profiles) and hf auth list (to list local profiles).

The legacy huggingface-cli remains active and fully-functional. We’re keeping it around to ease the transition. If you use any command from the legacy CLI, you’ll see a warning that points you to the new CLI equivalent:.

We couldn’t resist shipping our first dedicated command: hf jobs.

Hugging Face Jobs is a new service that lets you run any script or Docker image on Hugging Face Infrastructure using the hardware flavor of your choice. Billing is "pay-as-you-go", meaning you pay only for the seconds you use. Here’s how to launch your first command:.

XXRI-OS explores the lowest end of the Linux desktop

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (549 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Less is more, but this distro explores exactly how much less.
  • Fresh Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.
  • According to recent reports, XXRI OS is a fairly fresh desktop Linux distro.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less is more, but this distro explores exactly how much less.

Fresh Linux distros seem to appear daily, but far too few distinguish themselves by being smaller and simpler.

According to recent reports, XXRI OS is a fairly fresh desktop Linux distro. It has a snazzy-looking website, complete with an amusing URL, and along similar lines, its GitHub page has a very heavily formatted README. Nonetheless, this is not another over-complex opinionated slopfest of an OS with built-in AI, bizarre keystrokes, and several proprietary components. It's almost the reverse.

The main download is just 287.4 MB, and that's the full distro, not a minimalist installer that fetches most of the OS over your internet connection. We installed it in a VirtualBox VM. It took 675 MB of disk space, and in the graphical desktop, when we opened a terminal window, it reported just 75 MB of RAM in use with the desktop and terminal running. We are restraining ourselves hard when we say that those are unusually low numbers for the 2020s. We would expect most cut-down lightweight Linux distros to use around five to 10 times as much disk space or memory.

Recent findings suggest that the current release of XXRI-OS is version 2.7. XXRI OS 1.0 came out in May 2025, making this a young project with five published releases already behind it. It also has much deeper roots: it is based on the existing and much older Tiny Core Linux. The Reg FOSS desk last looked at Tiny Core Linux 15 back in March 2024 and the project is still going strong: the latest version is version 17.1.

Tiny Core Linux is a marvel, but there are prices to pay for somehow getting a graphical Linux desktop into a 23 MB download. It runs from RAM and uses its own extension-based package system, which can make adding components and managing updates unfamiliar territory. XXRI OS takes TCL and turns it into a slightly more conventional desktop.

Industry observers note that it installs to disk in the usual way, and it includes the core functions that most people would expect from their OS in 2026. It has a file manager, a text editor, a media player, a simple app store for adding further components, and a settings app including an update manager. It even includes its own web browser, and there are both x86-32 and x86-64 variants.

The desktop layout has a floating dock at bottom center, and the icons are unlabelled. To save you some guesswork, though, floating just to the left of the dock is an icon with a grid of dots, which is an app launcher. The icons in that do have text labels underneath, so you can learn which symbol denotes which function from here.

We plan to experiment more with this remarkable little OS and see how well it runs on the oldest, slowest boxes in the Irish Sea wing of Vulture Towers, but we like what we see so far. It's an impressive experiment in how low Linux can go and remain useful. While Tiny Core Linux goes down to Windows 95 levels of resource usage, XXRI OS has a more usable Windows 2000-level baseline. Over a quarter of a century later, that is nearly unbeatable. ®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • If you have trained your own machine learning model, you know how important it is to be able to track metrics, parameters, and hyperparameters during training and visualize them afterwards to better understand your training run.
