In a recent development, let's build a practical kernel that converts an image from RGB to grayscale. This example uses PyTorch's modern C++ API to register our function as a first-class, native operator.

A clean, predictable structure is the foundation of a good project. The Hugging Face Kernel Builder expects your files to be organized like this:.

Sources indicate that this file orchestrates the entire build. It tells the kernel-builder what to compile and how everything connects.

To ensure anyone can build your kernel on any machine, we use a flake.nix file. It locks the exact version of the kernel-builder and its dependencies, eliminating "it works on my machine" issues.

Now for the GPU code. Inside csrc/img2gray.cu, we'll define a kernel that uses a 2D grid of threads—a natural and efficient fit for processing images.

This is the most key step. We're not just binding to Python; we're registering our function as a native PyTorch operator. This makes it a first-class citizen in the PyTorch ecosystem, visible under the torch.ops namespace.

The file torch-ext/torch_binding.cpp handles this registration.

In simple terms, TORCH_LIBRARY_EXPAND allows us to define our operator in a way that can be easily extended or modified in the future.

This approach is crucial for two main reasons:.

Industry observers note that compatibility with torch.compile: By registering our kernel this way, torch.compile can "see" it. This allows PyTorch to fuse your custom operator into larger computation graphs, minimizing overhead and maximizing performance. It's the key to making your custom code work seamlessly with PyTorch's broader performance ecosystem.

In a recent development, hardware-Specific Implementations: This system allows you to provide different backends for the same operator. You could add another TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(img2gray, CPU, ...) block pointing to a C++ CPU function. PyTorch's dispatcher would then automatically call the correct implementation (CUDA or CPU) based on the input tensor's device, making your code powerful and portable.

Setting up the __init__.py wrapper.

In torch-ext/img2gray/ we need an __init__.py file to make this directory a Python package and to expose our custom operator in a user-friendly way.

The _ops module is auto-generated by kernel-builder from a template to provide a standard namespace for your registered C++ functions.

Recent findings suggest that once you have a ready-to-use kernel, there are some things you can do to make it easier to deploy your kernel. We will discuss using versioning as a tool to make API changes without breaking downstream use of kernels. After that, we will wrap up showing how you can make Python wheels for your kernel.

In a recent development, you might decide to upgrade your kernel after a while. Maybe you have found new ways of improving performance or perhaps you would like to extend the kernel's functionality. Some changes will require you to change the API of your kernel. For instance, a newer version might add a new mandatory argument to one of the public functions. This can be inconvenient to downstream consumers, because their code would break until they add this new argument.

A downstream user of a kernel can avoid such breakage by pinning the kernel that they use to a particular revision. For instance, since each Hub repository is also a Git repository, they could use a git commit shorthash to pin the kernel to a revision:.

Using a Git shorthash will reduce the chance of breakage; however, it is hard to interpret and does not allow graceful upgrades within a version range. We therefore recommend using the familiar semantic versioning system for Hub kernels. Adding a version to a kernel is easy: you simply add a Git tag of the form vx.y.z where x.y.z is the version. For instance, if the current version of the kernel is 1.1.2, you can tag it as v1.1.2. You can then get that version with get_kernel:.

Sources indicate that versioning becomes even more powerful with version bounds. In semantic versioning, the version 1.y.z, must not have backward-incompatible changes in the public API for each succeeding x and y. So, if the kernel's version was 1.1.2 at the time of writing your code, you can ask the version to be at least 1.1.2, but less than 2.0.0:.

It has been revealed that this will ensure that the code will always fetch the latest kernel from the 1.y.z series. The version bound can be a Python-style version specifier.

You can tag a version with huggingface-cli:.

It has been revealed that in large projects, you may want to coordinate the kernel versions globally rather than in each get_kernel call. Moreover, it is often useful to lock kernels, so that all your consumers have the same kernel versions, which aids handling bug reports.

The kernels library offers a nice way of managing kernels at the project-level. To do so, add the kernels package to the build-system requirements of your project, in the pyproject.toml file. After doing so, you can specify your project's kernel requirements in the tools.kernels section:.

It has been revealed that the version can be specified with the same type of version specifiers as Python dependencies. This is another place where the version tags (va.b.c) come handy -- kernels will use a repository's version tags to query what versions are available. After specifying a kernel in pyproject.toml, you can lock it to a specific version using the kernels command-line utility. This utility is part of the kernels Python package:.

According to recent reports, this generates a kernels.lock file with the latest kernel versions that are compatible with the bounds that are specified in pyproject.toml. kernels.lock should be committed to your project's Git repository, so that every user of the project will get the locked kernel versions. When newer kernels versions are released, you can run kernels lock again to upgrade the lock file.

You need one last bit to fully implement locked kernels in a project. The get_locked_kernel is the counterpart to get_kernel that uses locked kernels. So to use locked kernels, replace every occurrence of get_kernel with get_locked_kernel:.

The get_locked_kernel function will download the kernel when it is not available in the local Hub cache. This is not ideal for applications where you do not want to download binaries at runtime. For example, when you are building a Docker image for an application, you usually want the kernels to be stored in the image along with the application. This can be done in two simple steps.

First, use the load_kernel function in place of get_locked_kernel:.

As the name suggests, this function will only load a kernel, it will never try to download the kernel from the Hub. load_kernel will raise an exception if the kernel is not locally available. So, how do you make the kernels locally available? The kernels utility has you covered! Running kernels download . will download the kernels that are specified in kernels.lock. So e.g. in a Docker container you could add a step:.

and the kernels will get baked into your Docker image.

Kernels use the standard Hugging Face cache, so all HF_HOME caching rules apply.

We strongly recommend downloading kernels from the Hub using the kernels package. This has many benefits:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A person receives an automated decision that makes no sense to them. They ask for a review. Somewhere inside the organization, a policy names an accountable executive—but the support team cannot find anyone authorized to change the result. Governance exists on paper. The person is still stuck.

Industry observers note that that gap will become harder to defend in 2027. As AI moves into ordinary operations, accountability will have to become something an organization can exercise while a disputed decision is still affecting someone's life.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and OECD's 2026 due-diligence guidance already offer organizational foundations. My expectation for 2027 is that buyers will ask for evidence of these practices inside operating workflows. The following predictions concern organizational accountability, rather than a promise that a particular checklist can make every AI system fair.

The most revealing name on an AI governance chart is the person who can say stop. In 2027, more organizations will describe roles with genuine authority to suspend or change a deployment. That changes the meaning of ownership: responsibility becomes a decision right, with consequences for a project somebody else may be eager to keep running.

It has been revealed that responsibility without authority creates a ceremonial owner. A governance lead can maintain an inventory while a product team changes the model, a supplier changes the service, and an operations team changes the decision threshold. No single person necessarily controls the consequences of the resulting system.

According to recent reports, the Govern function in the NIST framework connects roles and organizational risk management. The NIST Playbook offers practical actions that organizations can adapt. These are voluntary resources, not evidence that adopters already execute them well.

The development I expect is a more concrete chain of authority: who can accept a use case, who can narrow its scope, and who can stop it when the evidence changes. Different decisions can belong to different roles. What matters is that the authority survives ordinary commercial pressure and is exercised against a documented standard. A well-written responsibility chart that nobody uses would not demonstrate the predicted change.

It has been revealed that look for published suspension criteria, records of actual governance decisions, and escalation paths beyond the product's revenue owner. A policy naming an accountable executive without explaining what that executive can change would provide weaker evidence than an operational case study.

According to recent reports, assign decision rights before expanding a deployment. Buyers should ask who can authorize exceptions and whether the risk function can halt a workflow without the supplier's consent. Founders can shorten enterprise reviews by making these responsibilities visible in the product and service agreement.

Industry observers note that an explanation can tell someone why a decision happened and still leave them powerless to correct it. I expect enterprise products to make challenges more practical in 2027, preserving the original evidence and recording what the reviewer decides. The test of the feature will be what happens after the person states the system has missed something important.

It has been revealed that an explanation and an appeal solve different problems. An explanation tells a person what supposedly happened. An appeal gives them a route to change an outcome that may be wrong, incomplete or inappropriate for their circumstances. A generic support form can satisfy neither need if the reviewer cannot reconstruct the original decision.

In a recent development, the OECD guidance treats due diligence as a continuing process involving impacts and responses. That makes remediation a useful commercial design question as well as an ethical one. My forecast is that some vendors will turn it into a repeatable workflow rather than leave each customer to improvise.

The difficult part will be the reviewer's independence and access to context. Re-running the same model with slightly different wording is not a meaningful challenge process. Nor should preserving evidence require indiscriminate retention of sensitive personal information. The system needs enough decision context to support correction while honoring appropriate retention and access limits.

Look for the ability to submit missing facts, reach a qualified human reviewer, and receive a recorded disposition. Reversal rates and time to correction will be more revealing than the existence of an appeal button. Unanswered queues would weaken the forecast's practical significance.

Industry observers note that budget for the people who handle contested decisions. A supplier's automation savings should be assessed alongside review workload and correction costs. Product teams should design evidence capture and access permissions with the appeal process, because reconstructing decisions afterward can be expensive or impossible.

An internal drafting assistant can become a customer-screening tool through a series of apparently small product decisions. The launch approval may still be on file while the use case has changed underneath it. In 2027, more governance programs will revisit material changes in models, data and affected populations, treating approval as a continuing responsibility.

Recent findings suggest that A system approved for drafting internal correspondence can become consequential when its output starts determining which customers receive an offer. The model may be unchanged; its social role has changed. Conversely, a supplier patch can alter behavior while the customer-facing workflow looks identical.

ISO/IEC 42001 addresses organizational AI management, and ISO's discussion of 42001 and impact assessment connects management practices with evaluating effects. Neither makes a management-system certificate a guarantee that every output is accurate or every deployment is acceptable.

According to recent reports, the practical challenge is proportionality. Repeating a full assessment for a spelling correction would overwhelm the process; ignoring a new affected population would undermine it. Organizations will need a defensible account of which changes alter the risk and which do not.

It has been revealed that look for specific reassessment triggers and examples where a deployment's conditions were narrowed after review. Version logs alone will be insufficient. Evidence that organizations compare real effects before and after a material change would strengthen this prediction considerably.

Include change notification and evaluation rights in supplier contracts. Internally, connect the model inventory to the systems that manage deployment changes. The objective is to identify changes that matter early enough to act, without turning every routine maintenance event into a board-level decision.

In a recent development, A certificate can become more reassuring than the evidence warrants. The harder commercial conversation is what it actually covers. In 2027, assurance and procurement documents will become clearer about the difference between an organization's management practices and the behavior of a particular deployment. That precision will make assurance more useful, even when it makes the sales claim less sweeping.

Sources indicate that the more popular a governance label becomes, the more tempting it is to treat that label as a universal seal of safety. Yet different assurance exercises answer different questions. An audit of management processes cannot prove that a model behaves reliably for a population the evaluator never tested.

ISO/IEC 42006 sets requirements for bodies auditing and certifying AI management systems. It is relevant to the quality of certification itself. It does not turn ISO/IEC 42001 into a product-performance benchmark. This distinction will become more commercially important as suppliers use assurance credentials in sales processes.

In a recent development, my confidence is lower here because incentives can favor broad reassurance over careful qualification. Still, sophisticated buyers have a reason to demand both organizational assurance and use-case evidence: they bear the consequences if a certified supplier's product fails in their workflow. Good assurance should make the remaining questions clearer, rather than imply that there are none.

Look for an explicit statement of the certified entity, scope, exclusions and validity period, alongside separate application testing. Claims that a certificate proves an AI system is unbiased or universally compliant would run against the direction predicted here.

Industry observers note that use certification to inform diligence, then evaluate the actual deployment. Suppliers should prepare a clear explanation of what their assurance covers. Buyers should ask which unresolved risks remain their responsibility and what evidence would justify accepting them.

Accountability becomes visible when the organization has a reason to resist it: an attractive launch, an expensive correction, a profitable use case that needs narrowing. The strongest governance stories in 2027 will show how those decisions were made—and whether the people affected had a meaningful way to be heard.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How to trade BTC, ETH, SOL, and XRP markets simultaneously while managing shared capital, portfolio exposure, and execution risk.

Recent findings suggest that building a market-making bot for a single Polymarket market is one challenge. Running the same strategy across multiple markets introduces an entirely different set of engineering problems.

Imagine your Python bot is already monitoring BTC 5-minute Up/Down markets.

Industry observers note that everything works reasonably well. Your bot receives order book updates, calculates quotes, places orders, and tracks inventory.

The obvious solution is to create four independent trading workers.

All four workers may be using the same trading capital, and their positions may be exposed to the same market movements.

Without centralized coordination, your bot can overallocate funds, accumulate excessive exposure, or submit orders that violate portfolio-wide risk limits.

In Day 18 of our Polymarket Market Maker Bot series, we'll explore how to build a coordinated multi-market trading architecture using Python.

A single-market bot has a relatively straightforward architecture.

When you expand to multiple markets, simply duplicating this architecture isn't enough.

Each strategy needs its own market-specific state, but certain resources must be shared across the entire trading system.

A better architecture looks like this:.

Each market strategy independently handles:.

Meanwhile, shared services handle:.

This separation allows you to expand without losing control of your overall portfolio.

Suppose your trading account contains 100 USDC.

You configure four trading bots:.

You only have $100, but your strategies collectively expect to use $160.

This creates a capital allocation problem.

And the situation becomes more complicated when you include open orders.

A strategy might have only $10 in filled positions but another $20 committed to pending buy orders.

Those orders may execute at any moment.

If multiple strategies independently assume that the same funds are available, the trading system can exceed its intended budget.

The solution is simple in principle:.

Every market must request capital from one shared capital manager before submitting fresh orders.

We'll start with a $100 trading budget.

Our illustrative allocation is:.

These values demonstrate the architecture rather than a recommended trading allocation.

Using Decimal is preferable to ordinary floating-point arithmetic for financial accounting.

The advantage of this approach is flexibility.

If your account budget increases or decreases, the allocation function can recalculate the market budgets automatically.

However, allocation alone doesn't prevent overspending.

We also need to track reserved capital.

Let's assume BTC has a $40 allocation.

In a real prediction-market system, the accounting must distinguish collateral committed to buy orders from YES/NO tokens reserved for sell orders.

Filled positions, outstanding orders, and account balances must also be reconciled against exchange state.

For now, we'll implement a simplified reservation manager.

This is an educational implementation, not a complete production ledger.

According to recent reports, in production, reservations must be atomic across concurrent workers. A shared database transaction or another concurrency-safe reservation mechanism is necessary to prevent two workers from spending the same available balance.

You must also reconcile order fills, cancellations, settlement events, and exchange balances.

Now let's separate the trading state of each market.

Every market needs its own inventory and order tracking.

We can now create separate instances:.

Each strategy can calculate its own quotes using its market's order book and inventory.

For example, the BTC strategy doesn't need to know how the ETH strategy calculates quotes.

But it does need permission from the shared risk system before executing an order.

That brings us to the most important component.

Imagine your bot right now has the following estimated exposures:.

Suppose your portfolio-wide exposure limit is $70.

Even if each individual strategy remains below its own market limit, the combined portfolio already exceeds the intended maximum.

A centralized risk manager must prevent additional exposure from being approved.

The trade would increase portfolio exposure from $60 to $75.

Because the limit is $70, the trade is rejected.

This example assumes that the proposed order increases exposure by the specified amount. A real risk engine must distinguish exposure-increasing trades from exposure-reducing trades.

It must also consider existing orders, collateral requirements, and the actual payoff structure of YES/NO positions.

The risk manager should be the final authority before an order reaches the execution layer.

Here's another vital issue.

BTC, ETH, SOL, and XRP are separate markets, but their underlying asset prices may respond to common market events.

For example, a sudden cryptocurrency market selloff could affect several assets simultaneously.

If your bot holds positions that lose value under the same scenario, the portfolio may suffer multiple losses at once.

Correlation describes the degree of linear relationship between two variables.

Its coefficient ranges from -1 to +1.

Consider these hypothetical values:.

These numbers are examples, not live market measurements.

This produces a correlation matrix for the sample returns.

For a production system, five observations are nowhere near enough.

You should use a larger historical dataset, align timestamps, handle missing data, and monitor rolling correlations.

There's also an important distinction:.

Correlation between cryptocurrency prices is not necessarily the same as correlation between prediction-market token returns or strategy profits.

For Polymarket risk management, you should evaluate the actual YES/NO positions and the outcomes that affect their value.

When several strategies run simultaneously, you need a consolidated portfolio view.

A useful monitoring system should track:.

Let's build a simple illustrative report.

Calculate a simple gross exposure indicator:.

This is a simplified accounting indicator, not a complete measure of economic risk.

For example, matched YES and NO positions may have different settlement characteristics than unmatched directional positions.

A production dashboard should display gross commitments, collateral usage, net exposure, and scenario-based risk separately.

Correlation analysis helps identify relationships between markets.

But correlation alone cannot tell you how your portfolio will behave during extreme conditions.

That's where stress testing becomes useful.

Suppose we have the following illustrative positions:.

We can estimate the change in value under this simplified scenario.

This illustrates a general valuation shock.

It does not directly model how Polymarket binary contracts settle.

A proper prediction-market stress engine should evaluate different YES/NO price and resolution scenarios, including trading fees and existing open-order commitments.

The important point is that you must test how the whole portfolio responds to adverse scenarios, not just each strategy individually.

So far, we've assigned fixed capital weights:.

One market may have deeper liquidity, while another may experience higher volatility or worse execution quality.

You may want to adapt capital allocations based on measurable market conditions.

Here's a basic scoring function:.

Calculate normalized allocation weights:.

These scores are hypothetical, and this formula is not a validated trading model.

Before using dynamic allocation in production, you need to establish hard minimum and maximum limits, evaluate historical performance, and prevent excessive rebalancing.

Most importantly, dynamic allocation must never bypass the central risk manager.

Our architecture is ready for multiple independent strategy instances.

Now we need a way to process them concurrently.

Python's asyncio library is useful for handling multiple market data streams and network operations.

Each market runs as an independent asynchronous task.

In a real implementation, the workers would process WebSocket updates, update order books, calculate quotes, and submit proposed orders to shared risk and execution services.

A reliable multi-market bot also needs:.

One failed market worker should not crash the entire trading system.

Likewise, a disconnected or stale market feed should prevent unsafe order submission for the affected market.

Let's combine the components into one coordinated architecture.

The order flow should work like this:.

Each market worker maintains an up-to-date view of its order book.

The strategy determines its desired price and size.

The central risk manager evaluates market and portfolio limits.

The capital manager atomically reserves the collateral or inventory needed for the order.

The execution layer communicates with the exchange.

Fills, cancellations, and failures enhancement the shared portfolio state.

The dashboard reflects current inventory, commitments, and risk.

This architecture is more maintainable than duplicating a complete independent trading system for every market.

Before expanding your bot, watch out for these mistakes.

Several strategies assume the same funds are available.

Solution: Use centralized, concurrency-safe reservations.

Risk calculations include filled positions but overlook pending orders.

Solution: Include open-order commitments in risk checks.

Several positions lose value under the same broader market event.

Solution: Monitor cross-market exposure and run portfolio stress scenarios.

Adding ten markets before validating two creates unnecessary complexity.

Solution: Expand gradually and verify reliability at every stage.

The bot restarts with incomplete knowledge of outstanding exchange orders.

Solution: Reconcile balances, orders, and positions before resuming trading.

If you already have a working single-market Polymarket bot, here's a reasonable sequence for extending it.

You don't need to build every component at once.

Start by making two markets operate safely under a shared budget.

Then add complexity only when the system demonstrates that it can handle the existing workload reliably.

Building a multi-market Polymarket bot isn't just about running more trading strategies.

It's about designing a system that understands the entire portfolio.

Each market should have its own strategy state, but all markets must share consistent capital accounting, execution coordination, and risk controls.

Independent strategies. Shared capital. Centralized risk. Coordinated execution.

That's the foundation for moving from a collection of trading scripts toward a more robust multi-market trading platform.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that zeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic.
  • This is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in.
  • The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that zeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic. It’s efficient, flexible, and ideal for demos but it doesn’t always make full use of everything the GPU and CUDA stack can offer. Generating images or videos can take a significant amount of time. Being able to squeeze out more performance, taking advantage of the H200 hardware, does matter in this case.

This is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in. Instead of compiling models on the fly (which doesn’t play nicely with ZeroGPU’s short-lived processes), AoT lets you optimize once and reload instantly.

The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.

Recent findings suggest that in this post, we’ll show how to wire up Ahead-of-Time (AoT) compilation in ZeroGPU Spaces. We'll explore advanced tricks like FP8 quantization and dynamic shapes, and share working demos you can try right away. If you cannot wait, we invite you to check out some ZeroGPU-powered demos on the zerogpu-aoti organization.

Pro owners and Team / Enterprise org members can create ZeroGPU Spaces, while anyone can freely use them (Pro, Team and Enterprise users get 8x more ZeroGPU quota).

Spaces is a platform powered by Hugging Face that allows ML practitioners to easily publish demo apps.

Typical demo apps on Spaces look like:.

This works great, but ends up reserving a GPU for the Space during its entire lifetime – even when it has no user activity.

When executing .to('cuda') on this line:.

It has been revealed that pyTorch initializes the NVIDIA driver, which sets up the process on CUDA forever. This is not very resource-efficient given that app traffic is not perfectly smooth, but is rather extremely sparse and spiky.

In a recent development, zeroGPU takes a just-in-time approach to GPU initialization. Instead of setting up the main process on CUDA, it automatically forks the process, sets it up on CUDA, runs the GPU tasks, and finally kills the fork when the GPU needs to be released.

Thanks to the Python spaces package, the only code change needed to get this behaviour is as follows:.

By importing spaces and adding the @spaces.GPU decorator, we:.

It has been revealed that zeroGPU at the moment allocates an MIG slice of H200 (3g.71gb profile). Additional MIG sizes including full slice (7g.141gb profile) will come in late 2025.

Modern ML frameworks like PyTorch and JAX have the concept of compilation that can be used to optimize model latency or inference time. Behind the scenes, compilation applies a series of (often hardware-dependent) optimization steps such as operator fusion, constant folding, etc.

PyTorch (from 2.0 onwards) currently has two major interfaces for compilation:.

torch.compile works great in standard environments: it compiles your model the first time it runs, and reuses the optimized version for subsequent calls.

However, on ZeroGPU, given that the process is freshly spun up for (almost) every GPU task, it means that torch.compile can’t efficiently re-use compilation and is thus forced to rely on its filesystem cache to restore compiled models. Depending on the model being compiled, this process takes from a few dozen seconds to a couple of minutes, which is way too much for practical GPU tasks in Spaces.

This is where ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation shines.

With AoT, we can export a compiled model once, save it, and later reload it instantly in any process, which is exactly what we need for ZeroGPU. This helps us reduce framework overhead and also eliminates cold-start timings typically incurred in just-in-time compilation.

According to recent reports, but how can we do ahead-of-time compilation on ZeroGPU? Let’s dive in.

Industry observers note that let's go back to our ZeroGPU base example and unpack what we need to enable AoT compilation. For the purpose of this demo, we will use the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev model:.

In the discussion below, we only compile the transformer component of pipe since, in these generative models, the transformer (or more generally, the denoiser) is the most computationally heavy component.

Compiling a model ahead-of-time with PyTorch involves multiple steps:.

Note that these are the same kinds of inputs we expect to see during the actual runs. To capture those inputs, we will leverage the spaces.aoti_capture helper from the spaces package:.

When used as a context manager, aoti_capture intercepts the call to any callable (pipe.transformer in our case), prevents it from executing, captures the input arguments that would have been passed to it, and stores their values in call.args and call.kwargs.

Now that we have example args and kwargs for our transformer component, we can export it to a PyTorch ExportedProgram by using torch.export.export utility:.

An exported PyTorch program is a computation graph that represents the tensor computations along with the original model parameter values.

Once the model is exported, compiling it is pretty straightforward.

A traditional AoT compilation in PyTorch often requires saving the model on disk so it can be later reloaded. In our case, we’ll leverage a helper function part of the spaces package: spaces.aoti_compile. It's a tiny wrapper around torch._inductor.aot_compile that manages saving and lazy-loading the model as needed. It's meant to be used like this:.

This compiled_transformer is now an AoT-compiled binary ready to be used for inference.

Now we need to bind our compiled transformer to our original pipeline, i.e., the pipeline.

It has been revealed that A naive and almost working approach is to simply patch our pipeline like pipe.transformer = compiled_transformer. Unfortunately, this approach does not work because it deletes crucial attributes like dtype, config, etc. Only patching the forward method does not work well either because we are then keeping original model parameters in memory, often leading to OOM errors at runtime.

spaces package provides a utility for this, too -- spaces.aoti_apply:.

Recent findings suggest that et voilà! It will take care of patching pipe.transformer.forward with our compiled model, as well as cleaning old model parameters out of memory.

To perform the first three steps (intercepting input examples, exporting the model, and compiling it with PyTorch inductor), we need a real GPU. CUDA emulation that you get outside of @spaces.GPU function is not enough because compilation is truly hardware-dependent, for instance, relying on micro-benchmark runs to tune the generated code. This is why we need to wrap it all inside a @spaces.GPU function and then get our compiled model back to the root of our app. Starting from our original demo code, this gives:.

With just a dozen lines of additional code, we’ve successfully made our demo quite faster (1.7x faster in the case of FLUX.1-dev).

If you want to learn more about AoT compilation, you can read PyTorch's AOTInductor tutorial.

Now that we have demonstrated the speedups one can realize under the constraints of operating with ZeroGPUs, we will discuss a few gotchas that came up while working with this setup.

AoT can be combined with quantization to deliver even greater speedups. For image and video generation, the FP8 post-training dynamic quantization schemes deliver good speed-quality trade-offs. However, FP8 requires a CUDA compute capability of at least 9.0 to work. Thankfully, for ZeroGPUs, since they’re based on H200s, we can already take advantage of the FP8 quantization schemes.

Images and videos can come in different shapes and sizes. Hence, it’s important to also account for shape dynamism when performing AoT compilation. The primitives provided by torch.export.export make it easily configurable to provide what inputs should be treated accordingly for dynamic shapes, as shown below.

Dynamic shapes is sometimes not enough when dynamism is too important.

In a recent development, this is, for instance, the case with the Wan family of video generation models if you want your compiled model to generate different resolutions. One thing can be done in this case: compile one model per resolution while keeping the model parameters shared and dispatching the right one at runtime.

Industry observers note that here is a minimal example of this approach: zerogpu-aoti-multi.py. You can also see a fully working implementation of this paradigm in the Wan 2.2 Space.

In a recent development, since the ZeroGPU hardware and CUDA drivers are perfectly compatible with Flash-Attention 3 (FA3), we can use it in our ZeroGPU Spaces to speed things up even further. FA3 works with ahead-of-time compilation. So, this is ideal for our case.

Sources indicate that compiling and building FA3 from source can take several minutes, and this process is hardware-dependent. As owners, we wouldn’t want to lose precious ZeroGPU compute hours. This is where Hugging Face kernels library comes to the rescue. It provides access to pre-built kernels that are compatible for a given hardware. For example, when we try to run:.

Recent findings suggest that it tries to load a kernel from the kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3 repository, which is compatible with the current setup. Otherwise, it will error out due to incompatibility complications. Luckily for us, this works seamlessly on the ZeroGPU Spaces. This means we can leverage the power of FA3 on ZeroGPU, using the kernels library.

Here is a fully working example of an FA3 attention processor for the Qwen-Image model.

So far, we have been compiling the full model. Depending on the model, full model compilation can lead to significantly long cold start times. Long cold start times make the development experience unpleasant.

We can also choose to compile regions within a model, significantly reducing the cold start times, while retaining almost all the benefits of full model compilation. Regional compilation becomes promising when a model has repeated blocks of computation. A standard language model, for example, has a number of identically structured Transformer blocks.

Sources indicate that in our example, we can compile the repeated blocks of the Flux transformer ahead of time, and propagate the compiled graph to the remaining repeated blocks. The Flux Transformer has two kinds of repeated blocks: FluxTransformerBlock and FluxSingleTransformerBlock.

You can check out this Space for a complete example.

💡 For Flux.1-Dev, switching to regional compilation reduces the compilation time from 6 minutes to just 30 seconds while delivering identical speedups.

It has been revealed that once a model (or even a model block) is compiled ahead of time, we can serialize the compiled graph module as an artifact and reuse later. In the context of a ZeroGPU-powered demo on Spaces, this will significantly cut down the demo startup time by skipping the compilation time.

To keep the storage light, we can just save the compiled model graph without including any model parameters inside the artifact.

Check out this collection that shows a full workflow of obtaining compiled model graph, pushing it to the Hub, and then using it to build a demo.

ZeroGPU within Hugging Face Spaces is a powerful feature that enables AI builders by providing access to powerful compute. In this post, we indicated how customers can benefit from PyTorch’s ahead-of-time compilation techniques to speed up their applications that leverage ZeroGPU.

We demonstrate speedups with Flux.1-Dev, but these techniques are not limited to just this model. Therefore, we encourage you to give these techniques a try and provide us with feedback in this community discussion.

#80944. Latency Is Bought At Training Time

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (773 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Latency Is Bought At Training Time

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As humanoid control strips out the conversion step between a person’s movement and a robot’s joints, the hard work moves upstream into the motion data those systems learn from.
  • Watch someone in a headset drive a humanoid robot and the first thing you notice is the delay.
  • Industry observers note that most of the beat is spent on translation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanoid control strips out the conversion step between a person’s movement and a robot’s joints, the hard work moves upstream into the motion data those systems learn from.

Watch someone in a headset drive a humanoid robot and the first thing you notice is the delay. The arm goes up, and a beat later the machine’s arm goes up. That beat decides whether an operator can catch a slipping box or stop a machine before it leans past the point of recovery.

Industry observers note that most of the beat is spent on translation. Human bodies and robot bodies do not match: limb lengths differ, joints swing through different ranges, weight sits in different places. Teleoperation systems usually bridge that difference with online retargeting, converting a human pose into a robot pose while the person is still moving. The conversion costs time, and it can hand the controller a target the machine physically cannot hold.

A recent preprint, Beyond Retargeting, takes the blunt route around that problem and removes the conversion. Its authors describe a policy that maps raw human motion straight to robot joint commands in a single forward pass, with no kinematic adaptation happening live. They pair it with a learned codebook of whole-body motion primitives, essentially a vocabulary of plausible movements, so that noisy or partial observations get projected onto something the robot can actually do and missing body parts get filled back in. Tested on a Unitree G1 in simulation and on hardware, driven by virtual reality, optical motion capture, text-generated motion and ordinary single-camera video, they report better latency and robustness than the baselines they compare against.

I think the headline hides the real trade. Removing a step at run time does not delete the work; it pushes it into training, where the model has to absorb in advance every bodily difference it used to compute on the fly. To me that makes responsiveness a property of the dataset as much as of the controller: the split second saved in a demo was purchased months earlier, in recorded human movement spanning different body shapes, speeds and sensor conditions. I would watch how gracefully systems like this hold up when the person driving them resembles nobody in the training corpus.

Sources indicate that snapping a strange observation onto the nearest plausible prototype is a safety feature when the library of prototypes is wide, and a failure mode when it is thin. A crouch nobody ever recorded becomes the closest thing that was recorded, and the robot performs that instead, confidently. Coverage of the motion library, not cleverness in the projection, sets the boundary of what the machine can be asked to do. The same logic applies across input channels: a clean optical capture and a shaky phone video of the identical movement have to land in the same place, which is a question about recording and labeling standards long before it is a question about architecture.

Corpora like that are a production problem more than a research problem, built from trained people, written standards and review passes that treat the thousandth record exactly like the first. Through Flipside, our Philippines-based operating subsidiary, we now own trained, managed, quality-controlled human capacity capable of meeting demanding production standards rather than renting it, together with established production pipelines, quality-management systems and institutional knowledge.[1] We are building this infrastructure with a particular opportunity in mind: embodied intelligence.[1].

Nothing in retargeting-free control reduces the need to watch real human beings move. The primitives come from captured motion. The text-to-motion generators that supply one of the input channels were themselves trained on captured motion. Even the claim that a system is robust is a claim about a distribution, and somebody assembled that distribution, decided what belonged in it and checked that the labels meant the same thing twice.

What I find clarifying about this line of work is that it makes the dependency impossible to hide. When a translation step sits between the person and the machine, you can tell yourself the step will absorb the mess. Take the step out and the mess arrives at the joints.

In a recent development, I think the field keeps arriving at the same answer from different directions. Every technique that makes a robot quicker or steadier in the moment is a technique that spends data earlier, and models are getting cheaper to train and easier to copy while the recorded account of how human bodies actually move is neither. The scarce thing was never the policy. It was the ground truth underneath it.

For disclosures, see this article on our website: https://nexscient.ai/latency-is-bought-at-training-time/#disclosure.

#80942. Kafka UI needs authorization beyond its login page

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (507 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Kafka UI needs authorization beyond its login page

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (507 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A Kafka UI can look like a convenience layer while behaving like a privileged cluster operator.
  • Sources indicate that the distinction matters most in smaller deployments where the UI runs beside the cluster and receives broad Kafka credentials.
  • Dynamic cluster configuration adds another boundary.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A Kafka UI can look like a convenience layer while behaving like a privileged cluster operator. It reads topic metadata, messages, consumer groups, ACLs, connectors, and sometimes the configuration that tells the UI where clusters are. A login page protects the browser session. It does not decide whether the service account behind that UI can delete a topic or change a consumer offset.

Sources indicate that the distinction matters most in smaller deployments where the UI runs beside the cluster and receives broad Kafka credentials. The UI may support OAuth, LDAP, or basic authentication, but those features authenticate people to the UI. The broker still sees the UI's Kafka principal. If that principal has broad ACLs, every user who can reach a powerful screen inherits part of that authority.

Dynamic cluster configuration adds another boundary. Kafka UI documentation describes DYNAMIC_CONFIG_ENABLED, which lets an operator add or modify clusters in the browser and stores the resulting configuration in dynamic_config.yaml. That is useful during installation. It is also a write path into the management plane. A public UI with weak access control can expose cluster bootstrap addresses, SASL settings, and deployment details that the operator intended to keep in configuration management.

Recent findings suggest that the built-in Swagger endpoint can widen the same surface. Documentation for the maintained project notes that SWAGGER_UI_ENABLED controls the API reference UI. Enable it only where the API is expected to be reachable. An endpoint that lists every operation is valuable to an attacker probing for topic writes, connector control, or ACL changes.

Kafka's own authorization model provides the durable boundary. The broker uses an authorizer to map an authenticated principal to allowed operations. The Apache Kafka security documentation is explicit that principals listed in super.owners bypass ACL checks and should be treated like root credentials. A Kafka UI should therefore use a dedicated principal with only the operations its users need. Give read-only teams a read-only path. Put cluster administration behind a separate deployment or a separate principal.

Sources indicate that there is also a deployment convenience trap. If the UI authenticates people but connects to Kafka with an administrator account, the UI can make a read-only person appear unable to see a topic while still allowing a direct API request to delete it. Test the effective path, not the button labels. Remove delete, topic-alter, ACL, and connector permissions from the service principal. Then verify that the UI returns a clear denial rather than silently retrying with another connection.

Operators should inventory four things together: who can sign in to the UI, which Kafka principal the UI uses, which ACLs that principal has, and which network paths can reach the UI. Restrict the listener to an administration network, terminate TLS at a trusted boundary, disable dynamic configuration after the initial setup where possible, and turn off Swagger unless it has its own protection.

A login screen answers who is using the interface. Kafka ACLs answer what the interface can do. Both need to be correct.

#80941. Breaking: SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1227 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data.
  • SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines.
  • It has been revealed that AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of new drugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data. This dataset is now available on Hugging Face, and for the first time, researchers have open access to more than 5 million AI‑generated, high‑accuracy protein-ligand 3D structures, each paired with validated empirical binding potency data.

SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines. More than just a dataset, SAIR is a strategic asset that bridges the long-standing data gap in AI-powered drug design. It empowers pharmaceutical, biotech, and tech‑bio leaders to accelerate R&D, expand target horizons, and supercharge AI models – moving more of the costly, lengthy drug design and optimization from the wet lab to in silico. This means shorter hit‑to‑lead timelines, more efficient lead optimization, fewer dead‑end projects, and a more predictable path from initial idea to clinical candidate.

It has been revealed that AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of new drugs. For decades, scientists have dreamed about AI that could identify or design a potent, non-toxic, and efficacious compound from a prompt describing the disease pathway, practically compressing years of drug R&D into a few minutes on a computer. However, this vision is bottlenecked by AI's ability to predict critical drug properties like potency, toxicity, etc., based solely on its molecular structure.

Sources indicate that furthermore, traditional structure‑based discovery is often slowed early by the determination of reliable 3D structures. Three‑dimensional molecular structure dictates a molecule’s functionality, dynamics and interactions, which is especially important when a potential drug candidate is expected to bind to a human protein target.

Experimental methods, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, require extensive time and investment, and many promising disease targets still lack experimentally validated structural information. Computer simulations have helped lower the barrier of getting 3D structures and predicting binding affinity. However, earlier generations of algorithms for protein folding and docking (like AlphaFold and Vina respectively) only predict static snapshots of molecules and proteins (which, in reality, are inherently dynamic and shape-changing).

SAIR solves that constraint by compiling over 1 million unique computationally co-folded protein–ligand pairs, ultimately yielding 5.24 million distinct 3D complexes (five different co-folded structures per pair). Each structure is paired with a curated IC₅₀ measurement from ChEMBL or BindingDB, providing for the first time a scalable link between high-quality 3D structures and drug potency, and bridging the historic data gap that has hindered AI-driven discovery. Deep-learned affinity models such as Boltz-2, trained on similar data, have been shown to yield up to a 1,000x speed-up over the traditional, first-principle approach.

According to recent reports, creating SAIR was a major feat of high-performance AI computing. It took more than 130,000 GPU hours to compute the SAIR dataset using Boltz1, a cofolding AI model, on a cluster of 760 NVIDIA H100 processors, leveraging the NVIDIA DGX Cloud through Google Cloud Platform.

Capturing highly granular node, operator, scheduler, and GPU metrics, as well as a close collaboration on both infrastructure and workload optimization, helped NVIDIA AI Accelerator and SandboxAQ engineering teams identify bottlenecks and optimize configurations to achieve the highest workload throughput.

Consequently, the two teams were able to achieve > 95% GPU compute utilization for generating the SAIR dataset. This enabled us to create SAIR in three weeks – as opposed to the original estimate of three months (more than a 4X speed up) – and resulted in a highly optimized, GPU-native computational workflow that seamlessly integrates with today’s cutting-edge enterprise compute environments.

According to recent reports, generating such a massive volume of data is only half the story. Equally important is confidence in its quality, which is why every predicted complex underwent rigorous validation with PoseBusters, an industry-standard, open-source tool for benchmarking structure-related AI in drug discovery. This tool checks chemical sanity and physical plausibility.

Industry observers note that the end result was that 97 percent of SAIR’s structures passed all checks. In addition to PoseBusters validation, we benchmarked leading affinity prediction methods, such as empirical scoring functions, 3D CNNs, and graph neural networks, across SAIR’s synthetic structures and experimental IC₅₀ values. The detailed results of these studies are available in our scientific manuscript on bioRxiv.

SAIR data is a reliable foundation for benchmarking new models as well as downstream modelling, screening, and design.

A persistent challenge in drug discovery is the “dark proteome,” or disease‑relevant proteins for which experimental structures simply do not exist. SAIR illuminates these uncharted regions by providing credible, AI‑predicted complexes wherever experimental data is scarce. For example, more than 40 percent of the proteins in the SAIR dataset have no available structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) whatsoever, with or without a ligand. SAIR addresses one of the biggest challenges with existing AI models, low generalizability due to data scarcity. With SAIR, scientists can now explore targets that were previously deemed undruggable, armed with structural hypotheses to guide virtual screening and lead optimization using trustworthy model predictions.

Recent findings suggest that moreover, SAIR’s cross‑target breadth uncovers polypharmacology patterns and elucidates how a single molecule might interact with multiple proteins. Leveraging this rich tapestry of interactions, you can train AI models to predict off‑target effects or identify new repurposing opportunities, equipping your organization with a deeper understanding of compound profiles before any lab work begins.

SAIR is freely available on Hugging Face. Here’s a quick guide to pull SAIR from Hugging Face, peek at the main table, and (optionally) download a few structure archives.

We use the Hub to fetch files and pandas+pyarrow to read the Parquet.

This grabs the file from the Hub and loads it into a DataFrame.

Structure files are shipped as many .tar.gz archives under structures_compressed/. List them and pick what you need.

Recent findings suggest that each archive can be large (≈10 GB). Download only the ones you need and extract them locally.

It has been revealed that A full version of this script, including more robust logging and validation, is available in the README file for your convenience. For more details, visit the SAIR homepage, read our manuscript on bioRxiv, or watch our 25-minute joint webinar with NVIDIA, where we demonstrate SAIR and explain how data is structured within it. Extensive documentation, tutorials, and example benchmarks are available to facilitate its use and accelerate internal adoption.The future of drug discovery is data-driven, AI-accelerated, and grounded in scalable, high-quality structural insights. While we don’t yet have AI that can design effective drug therapies with just a prompt, SAIR brings researchers ever closer to that goal with latest data and insights that can potentially shave years from even AI-accelerated R&D pipelines.We can’t wait to see what researchers will build using SAIR, and SandboxAQ experts are here to support them throughout the discovery process.

Contact the authors or post on the SAIR dataset discussion page.

Authors: Arman Zaribafiyan, Georgia Channing, Zane Beckwith, and Rudi Plesch.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When running a high-traffic bilingual (Arabic RTL / English LTR) Laravel 11 application serving enterprise B2B portals and diagnostic tools, server response time (TTFB — Time to First Byte) directly dictates both Core Web Vitals (LCP) and search engine crawl efficiency.

Here is the exact production engineering checklist our team at MTM4WEB used to bring median TTFB down from 1,277ms (with 9s spikes) to 60–120ms on a live Nginx + PHP 8.3-FPM stack.

On many HestiaCP / cPanel reverse-proxy setups, static files inside public_html/public accidentally pass through a rewrite or backend hop if the Nginx location block doesn't resolve the /public root directly.

Serving static assets (.css, .js, .webp, .woff2) directly from Nginx with long immutable cache headers eliminates unnecessary backend worker contention:.

When pm = ondemand is used with a low pm.max_children = 5, concurrent bursts (especially when search engine crawlers and consumers hit the site simultaneously) force requests to queue while FPM forks upcoming children.

Switching to a warm dynamic pool keeps workers ready in RAM:.

Never leave production running uncached configuration or debug listeners:.

Combined with PHP 8.3 OPcache (opcache.enable=1, opcache.memory_consumption=256), route resolution and config lookup drop to single-digit milliseconds.

If your application logs visitor analytics to MySQL on every request via middleware, bots probing 404 URLs or polling AJAX endpoints will flood your database with synchronous INSERT queries. Guard your middleware so it only logs real HTML 200 OK pageviews and skips /api/* and error responses.

Instead of manually updating hundreds of database rows after batch-converting legacy PNG/JPG assets to WebP with cwebp -q 82, you can transparently upgrade your Eloquent model accessor:.

You can test your own server's TTFB, HTTP compression headers, and DNS health using our free engineering tools:.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The latest AirPods, the AirPods 5, start at around $129.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirPods are expensive, but there are better ways to get them cheaper than the used market.

According to recent reports, ever since Apple removed the classic 3.5mm headphone jack, AirPods have taken center stage. While you can expect your AirPods to last a good while, nothing lasts forever. You'll eventually need upcoming AirPods if you want to stick with the wireless zeitgeist. Still, it's better to think twice before buying used AirPods to save a quick buck.

The latest AirPods, the AirPods 5, start at around $129. Other than switching to wired headphones or more affordable AirPod alternatives, you may have to wait for a price drop to grab a pair on a budget. And while second-hand tech is a great way to get expensive stuff on the cheap, this doesn't necessarily apply to AirPods.

The biggest concern with used AirPods is hygiene. AirPods that have spent their last life stuck in someone else's ears will be rife with earwax and other skin oils if they haven't been given a proper clean. Apple Support publishes guidelines on how to clean AirPods with methods for each model, so it is possible to pick up a used pair that's completely hygienic. But this doesn't mean any old seller will have done their due diligence, and it's not obvious whether a used pair has been rigorously cleaned or if it's just had its obvious gunk removed.

Recent findings suggest that second-hand AirPods also use standard lithium-ion batteries, which lose capacity over time as each charge cycle ages them. Where this becomes a special risk is that, unlike iPhones, there's no way to know how long your AirPod battery will last. This makes it easy for scammers to charge you too much for a pair near death's door.

In a recent development, these issues and others, such as the plethora of fakes on the market, make buying used AirPods a gamble. Another problem with buying used is that there are many ways to save on AirPods without going pre-owned. While used pairs can be deeply discounted, there's only a small gap in savings between taking that plunge and buying smart.

There are still a lot of upcoming and sealed AirPods on the market. The recently discontinued (but still supported) AirPods 4 can be found for a reasonable price on sites like eBay and Amazon, still in their unopened packaging, which is a safer way to save.

#80936. Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's latest efficient embedding model

📅 04 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2722 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's latest efficient embedding model

📅 04 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases.
  • Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent.
  • It has been revealed that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases. Designed for speed and efficiency, the model features a compact size of 308M parameters and a 2K context window, unlocking newly introduced possibilities for mobile RAG pipelines, agents, and more. EmbeddingGemma is trained to support over 100 languages and is the highest-ranking text-only multilingual embedding model under 500M on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) at the time of writing.

Text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent. These vectors enable fast similarity search, clustering, classification, and retrieval across massive corpora, powering everything from recommendation engines and semantic search to retrieval-augmented generation and code‑search tools. Embedding models that calculate these embeddings are widely used, with well over 200 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet. With just 308M parameters, a 2k‑token context window, and support for over 100 languages, EmbeddingGemma delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB) while staying under 200 MB of RAM when quantized.

The various design choices result in a very practical, open-source tool for computing high-quality multilingual embeddings on everyday devices.

In this blogpost, we describe the EmbeddingGemma architecture and training, and show you how to use the model with various frameworks like Sentence Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, txtai, Transformers.js, Text Embedding Inference, and ONNX.

Afterwards, we demonstrate how to finetune EmbeddingGemma on your domain for even stronger performance. In our example, we finetune EmbeddingGemma on the Medical Instruction and Retrieval Dataset (MIRIAD). The resulting model, sentence-transformers/embeddinggemma-300m-medical, achieves state-of-the-art performance on our task: retrieving passages of scientific medical papers in response to detailed medical questions. It even outperforms models twice as massive on this task.

In a recent development, embeddingGemma builds on the Gemma3 transformers backbone, but modified to use bi-directional attention instead of causal (one-way) attention. This means that earlier tokens in the sequence can attend to later tokens, effectively turning the architecture from a decoder into an encoder. Encoder models can outperform LLMs, which are decoders, on embedding tasks like retrieval (Weller et al., 2025). With this backbone, the model can process a sizable 2048 tokens at once, sufficient for typical retrieval inputs, especially given that larger inputs often result in information loss in the text embeddings.

Beyond the fresh Gemma3-based encoder backbone, which produces token embeddings, a mean pooling layer converts these token embeddings into text embeddings. Lastly, two dense layers transform the text embeddings into their final form, a 768-dimensional vector.

The EmbeddingGemma model has been trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing you to truncate the 768‑dimensional output to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions on demand. This results in faster downstream processing and lower memory and disk space utilization. See the Sentence Transformers usage for a snippet showing how to perform this truncation.

It has been revealed that the model has been trained using a carefully curated, multilingual corpus totalling approximately 320 billion tokens. The proprietary dataset is a blend of publicly available web text, code and technical documentation, and synthetic task‑specific examples. It has been filtered to avoid Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), sensitive data, and low-quality or unsafe content.

Sources indicate that embeddingGemma was benchmarked on the MMTEB (Multilingual, v2) and MTEB (English, v2) suites, which span a wide range of tasks, domains, and languages. Despite its modest 308M‑parameter size, the model consistently beats comparable baselines while keeping a very small memory footprint.

The results will be listed on the official MTEB Leaderboard. We exclude any model that has been trained on more than 20% of the MTEB data, to mitigate potential over‑fitting.

The demo can also be experienced in full screen.

Experience the demo yourself on a Desktop device.

Industry observers note that embeddingGemma is integrated with many popular tools, making it easy to incorporate into your existing workflows and applications. The model has been integrated in Sentence Transformers, and thus also in projects that use Sentence Transformers behind the scenes, such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai. See the examples below to get started with your preferred framework.

For production deployments, you can use Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) to serve the model efficiently on various hardware configurations, and you can use Transformers.js for use in web applications.

Industry observers note that regardless of your framework choice, you should be mindful of the prompts. For embedding models, prompts are prepended to the input text to allow the model to distinguish between different tasks. EmbeddingGemma was trained with these prompt names and prompts, so they should also be included when using the model:.

In Sentence Transformers, the query and document prompts are used automatically when calling model.encode_query and model.encode_document, but for other frameworks you might have to: $.

Because google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with MRL, the embeddings generated by this model can be truncated to lower dimensionalities without considerably hurting the evaluation performance. Embeddings with lower dimensionalities are both cheaper to store on disk and in memory, as well as faster for downstream tasks like retrieval, clustering, or classification.

In Sentence Transformers, you can set a lower dimensionality using the truncate_dim parameter on either the SentenceTransformer initialization or when calling model.encode/model.encode_query/model.encode_document:.

Note that the ranking is preserved despite using 3x smaller embeddings compared to the full-sized embeddings.

In a recent development, if you prefer, you can also use the LangChain HuggingFaceEmbeddings, which uses Sentence Transformers behind the scenes. Note that you'll have to tell LangChain to use the prompts called "query" and "document" for queries and documents, respectively. You can easily deploy EmbeddingGemma for both development and production using Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) version 1.8.1 or later.

Industry observers note that if you run the Docker container with the cuda-1.8.1 tag, it includes support for multiple GPU architectures: Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper. For a lighter image tailored to just your GPU, you can instead use a specific tag such as turing-1.8.1, 1.8.1 and 86-1.8.1 (Ampere), 89-1.8.1 (Ada Lovelace), or hopper-1.8.1.

Once deployed, regardless of the device or runtime, you can leverage the /v1/embeddings endpoint based on the OpenAI Embeddings API Specification to generate embeddings.

Alternatively, you can also leverage the /embed endpoint from the Text Embeddings Inference Embeddings API, which supports the prompt_name parameter, meaning there’s no need to manually prepend the prompt to the inputs but select it via prompt_name instead.

Additionally, note that since google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), you can also leverage the dimensions parameter, on both /v1/embeddings and /embed, to truncate the embeddings to lower dimensionalities (512, 256, and 128) without hurting the evaluation performance.

In a recent development, you can also run the model directly with ONNX Runtime, making it highly portable and cross-platform compatible. The example below demonstrates usage in Python, but the same approach can be applied in other languages (Java, C#, C++, etc.) as well.

As with all models compatible with the Sentence Transformers library, EmbeddingGemma can be easily fine-tuned on your specific dataset. To showcase this, we'll be finetuning google/embeddinggemma-300m on the Medical Instruction and RetrIeval Dataset (MIRIAD) dataset, such that our finetuned model becomes particularly adept at finding passages up to 1000 tokens from scientific medical papers given detailed medical questions. These passages can be used as crucial context for a generative model to answer questions more effectively.

In a recent development, below, you can explore each key component of the finetuning process using expandable tabs. Each tab contains the relevant code and a detailed explanation.

According to recent reports, this code loads the EmbeddingGemma model from Hugging Face, with optional model card metadata for documentation and sharing. The SentenceTransformer class loads the model weights and configuration, while the model_card_data argument attaches metadata useful for inclusion in the automatically generated model card.

This code loads the MIRIAD dataset, or rather, a copy that has been divided into train, eval, and test splits. Using a large, high-quality dataset ensures the model learns meaningful representations, while subsetting allows for faster experimentation. The load_dataset function fetches the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets, and the .select() method limits the number of samples for each split.

This code defines the loss function for training, using Cached Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (CMNRL). CMNRL is effective for retrieval tasks, as it uses in-batch negatives to efficiently train the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. The loss takes question-answer pairs and treats other answers in the batch as negatives, maximizing the distance between unrelated pairs in the embedding space. The mini_batch_size parameter controls the memory usage, but does not affect the training dynamics.

In a recent development, it's recommended to use this loss with a large per_device_train_batch_size in SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments and a low mini_batch_size in CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss for a strong training signal with low memory usage. Additionally, the NO_DUPLICATES batch sampler is recommended to avoid accidental false negatives.

Recent findings suggest that this code sets up all hyperparameters and configuration for training, evaluation, and logging. Proper training arguments are crucial for efficient, stable, and reproducible training. The arguments control batch sizes, learning rate, mixed precision, evaluation and saving frequency, and more. Notably, the prompts dictionary maps dataset columns to prompts used by the model to distinguish queries from documents.

This code sets up an evaluator for information retrieval, using queries and a corpus to measure model performance. Evaluation during training helps monitor progress and avoid overfitting. The evaluator computes retrieval metrics (NDCG, MRR, Recall, Precision, MAP, etc.) by checking if the model retrieves the correct passages for each query. It can be run before, during, and after training, and the results will be logged and incorporated in the automatically generated model card.

Note that this snippet in particular uses all (1k) evaluation questions against a corpus of all (1k) evaluation passages and 30k training passages, for a total of 31k documents. Evaluating only against evaluation passages is too simple for the model.

This code initializes and runs the training loop, coordinating all components.

Below is the complete script, combining all components above:.

Recent findings suggest that we ran the full training script on an RTX 3090 with 24GB of VRAM, and the completed training and evaluating scripts took 5.5 hours. If desired, you can further reduce the memory footprint by reducing mini_batch_size on the CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss and batch_size on the InformationRetrievalEvaluator instances. See here the logs from our training run:.

The performance of the base model was already excellent, with a strong 0.8340 NDCG@10 on our MIRIAD test set. Despite that, we were able to increase it considerably on this domain-specific dataset.

Our fine-tuning process achieved a significant improvement of +0.0522 NDCG@10 on the test set, resulting in a model that comfortably outperforms any existing general-purpose embedding model on our specific task, at this model size. Additional time and compute investment would allow for even stronger results, such as hard negatives mining or training with more than 100k data pairs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Designers hand you a brand hex like #3B82F6-ish, and your Tailwind config has 11 shades per color. Which one is "closest"? Eyeballing it leads to inconsistent UIs.

Sources indicate that euclidean distance in RGB treats all channels equally, but human vision doesn't. Two colors can be numerically close and look different (especially in greens). A better approach is to compare in a perceptual space such as CIELAB (deltaE).

Industry observers note that nearest shade is only half the story. Check the text/background pair against WCAG 4.5:1 for body text. A shade that matches the brand but fails contrast needs a darker neighbor for text.

I built a free, client-side tool that does the matching in your browser (nothing uploaded): Colors to Tailwind. Pair it with the contrast checker to validate accessibility.

Tech Report: A tempo slider that's off by default: half time, double time and a 90 BPM starting point

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev
